speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CONTAMINATION OF HEAVY WATER AT CHALK RIVER PLANT
speechtext: Yes. The account that was given to the press last evening is quite correct. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the
unavoidable and greatly regretted absence of the Postmaster General, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the report in the press today of the third large post office theft in the province of Ontario, making the total in that province alone some $200,000 in the last nine months, will the Prime Minister consider the advisability of an inquiry into the security methods of the post office? I need not point out that we have had presented to us the evidence of a widespread series of thefts right across the country. The circumstances are such that it would seem consideration should be given to the general problem of security for the protection of the post office staff themselves as well as the public treasury.
Righl Hon. L. S. St. Laureni (Prime Minister):	I can assure the Leader of the
Opposition that the security measures taken by the post office are under constant review. Every time a theft occurs the circumstances of the case are considered and serious consideration is given by the R.C.M.P. to the security measures in existence and to the question as to whether or not what has happened in an individual case would indicate some possibility of improving the safeguard against similar occurrences.
We all regret that there should be any thefts at all in the post office, but hon. gentlemen will well know that the losses due to thefts in the post office are quite insignificant when compared with the losses that occur in banks. I think the security measures taken by the post office are quite as efficient as those taken by the banks, and I think those that are taken by the banks are dictated by the prudent wisdom of the Canadian Bankers' Association to do everything possible to avoid those thefts, even though the cost of the security measures might exceed the probable losses that can arise from crimes of that nature. I think it is in the public interest not to be parsimonious in expenditures made to avoid the occasions and possibilities of those crimes. They are not crimes against individual institutions; they are crimes against the Canadian public.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SECURITY MEASURES TO PREVENT THEFTS
speechtext:
Will the Prime Minister not agree that there is a very marked difference between the situation of the banks and the

post office? The banks are called upon to handle cash in large quantities for the convenience of their customers and also for payrolls. Similar circumstances do not arise in connection with post offices and I would think that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) would agree that the circumstances are entirely different and that a comparison for that reason cannot be made. I would hope that the Prime Minister would give consideration to the desirability of some special inquiry into this whole matter of security because of the problem it raises for the staffs of our post offices as well as for those who might be affected by the direct robbery.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SECURITY MEASURES TO PREVENT THEFTS
speechtext: Special inquiry is going on all the time and I do not know of any better method of making inquiry and considering the system in force than the very close co-operation that exists between the post office authorities and the R.C.M.P. With respect to the comparison with the banks, of course individual cases frequently involve much more money when a robbery is committed against a bank than when it is committed against a post office. However, it is a matter of degree and the essentials of the operations are much the same whatever be the amount of loot secured.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SECURITY MEASURES TO PREVENT THEFTS
speechtext: I do not wish to extend this unduly, but I would point out that in Welland recently a theft amounted to $78,000. That seems to be a substantial sum by any test, and particularly it seems to be a very large sum to be on hand in a post office when the demands for available cash and money orders or other negotiable property would not seem to be of that scale.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SECURITY MEASURES TO PREVENT THEFTS
speechtext: Of course, the cash would represent both the sale of stamps and money deposited with the post office against money orders that are purchased by those who want to forward money in a manner that involves the guarantee of safety for the person concerned by the Post Office Department.

Mr. Chairman, last evening the hon. member for Mackenzie referred to an argument which had developed between himself and the hon. member for Churchill some months ago when the bill in regard to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources was before the house. The controversy seemed to centre around a report issued by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys on December 10, 1953, relative to the process of ore separation used by the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company of Flin Flon. The hon. member was good enough to send a copy of that report over to me last evening and I have now had time to read it and would make the following comment.
In 1921 the mines branch made preliminary laboratory scale tests on the treatment of Flin Flon ore. This gave promising results indicating that a satisfactory separation process could be achieved. In 1925, the Whitney interests of New York acquired the property. In a paper entitled "History of Development and Organization at Flin Flon Mine, Manitoba", prepared by Mr. W. A. Green of the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company and published in the transactions of the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, the following statements are made:
Results of small experimental tests which we (Whitney interests) had made on the ore prior to the examination of the property (in June 1925) led us to believe that a satisfactory treatment might be obtained.
Having assured ourselves of the presence of the ore and available power, our next step was to prove, by more extensive laboratory tests, the correctness of our belief that a successful method of treatment for the ore could be worked out. Accordingly, 300 tons of ore was shipped from Flin Flon to Denver, Colorado, to the research laboratories of the Metals Exploration Company, a company belonging to the Whitney interests.
A report of Mr. S. P. Lowe, who carried out the experimental work, contains the following quotation:
Flotation testing of Flin Flon ore was started in the Denver laboratory of Complex Ore Recoveries Company in March 1926. There had been a considerable amount of flotation testing previously which had shown possibilities of success, and it
6780	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys was felt that, with the increased knowledge of flotation and the comparatively new reagents then available, flotation held out the best prospects for a successful treatment of this ore.
The pilot plant runs, treating two tons a day, were completed on July 1, 1926, and on August 1, 1926, it was decided to instal a 25-ton pilot flotation plant at Flin Flon.
This (pilot) mill was operated until March 10, 1928, treating ore from various parts of the mine. The pilot plant was started again in July 1928, and operated until February 1929, when it was permanently shut down.
It was found that before an efficient separation of the economic minerals was obtained, the removal of talc was a necessity. This was in line with the recommendations made by the mines branch in 1922.
Thus although the preliminary tests were made by the mines branch, the pilot plant tests which led to the establishment of the 3,000-ton mill at Flin Flon were carried out by the company. It is obvious, therefore, that the final result was a joint effort in which the mines branch made a significant preliminary contribution, but the final result was brought about by tests and pilot plant operation on the part of the company.
The hon. member for Mackenzie also referred to a speech made by me at Flin Flon on February 24, 1954. He alleged that I repudiated the report of the mines branch and took the part of the hon. member for Churchill in this argument. I was able to find the notes of my speech, and the following is an extract from the introductory remarks which I made at that time. I was speaking of the hon. member for Churchill, who represents that riding, and I said the following:
Those of you who follow Hansard will know that Mr. Weaver earlier in the present session of parliament tangled with an opposition member. In his address to the House of Commons, your member was able to accomplish what few of us would dare to even attempt. He left everyone quite happy, including the mines branch and his parliamentary opponent. That sort of thing, after all, is the acid test of statesmanship.

When this ore was discovered there was no known process that would enable any mining corporation in Canada or the United States to separate these valuable deposits

Mr. Chairman, one of the responsibilities of the Secretary of State is the handling of parliamentary returns asked for by this house. I have noticed from time to time that there seems to be considerable delay between the times returns are first asked for officially by this house and the time the information becomes available, and I have wondered whether these delays are necessary. From time to time I have noticed also that the information tabled by the Secretary of State in answer to a return is far removed from what one would expect in answer to the specific questions posed in the return. I think that with respect to these parliamentary returns the Secretary of State has been from time to time somewhat less efficient and capable than we would hope. I am going
[Mr. Herridge.l
to select a particular return made at my request as an example of what happens.
The original questions were made an order for return on March 10, 1955. Those questions asked for certain information about the travelling expenses of ministers. The return was tabled on June 23, a lapse of three and a half months. The information contained in the return enables us to see approximately what happened. In the first place there was two weeks' delay between the time the order for return was passed by this house and the time the Secretary of State passed it on to the departments, because he requested this information under date of March 23. We find next that the departments concerned were exceedingly lax in sending back their information to the Secretary of State. As far as I can see, no attempts whatever were made to follow up. Let me give the committee the details of when this information was returned to the Secretary of State, keeping in mind the fact that he requested it on March 23.
We find that the Department of Labour replied promptly the next day on March 24 and sent in their information. Then we find that the next return came three weeks later on April 15 from trade and commerce. Then defence production on April 28; the Prime Minister's office on May 26; external affairs on June 6; transport on June 7; finance on June 17; national defence on June 23. In other words, we have a situation where the Secretary of State requested certain information and when it was not forthcoming apparently he or his department did nothing about prodding the departments to obtain this information. I would point out also that two additional departments made returns which did not even bear a date to indicate when the information was forwarded to the Secretary of State. I would suggest that it was at least his responsibility to have checked back in those particular cases to see that the information sent to him was dated. Furthermore, I would point out to you that I have listed only 12 departments. An additional eight departments did not reply to the question in any way whatsoever. They are the departments of citizenship and immigration, fisheries, justice, mines and technical surveys, national revenue, post office, public works and veterans affairs.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Does the hon. member say there was no answer at all or that a negative answer was offered by these departments?

That is the point I was coming to. I said in these particular cases there was no answer at all, not a negative answer. I am very glad the minister asks me to emphasize that. It is

possible to argue in respect to certain questions that they obviously do not apply to certain departments, and the Secretary of State could be justified under those circumstances in using his discretion and saying that these departments did not reply because the question obviously is not applicable. But at this point let me put on the record the particular question concerned in this order for return, in order that we can see whether or not a reply, either affirmatively containing information or negatively indicating that no information was available, would be expected. The question was in two parts:
1.	Between January 1, 1954 and January 31, 1955, how many trips, paid for in whole or in part by the public treasury and/or using transport supplied by the public service, or national defence department, were made by ministers of the crown to points other than in Canada?
2.	For each trip (a) who made it; (b) to where; (c) for what purpose; (d) what expenses were collected from the public treasury in respect thereof; (e) if national defence or other publicly owned transport was involved, between what points was it used?
That obviously is a return which could apply to any minister of the crown. One would logically expect that every minister of the crown would answer it. I can point out to the Secretary of State that in at least one case the fact that a negative return was not received and that no return was received meant that certain of the information requested was not tabled in this house.
The Minister of Public Works had made extensive travels in Europe during the period covered by this return. His department made no attempt whatsoever to reply to this request for information. Subsequently, when the return was tabled, I made an attempt to find out why this was so, by means of personal conversations. I do not think there is any objection to pointing out to the house at this point the reason. The Minister of Public Works felt that, since he had gone to Europe on behalf of the Department of Trade and Commerce, they should make the return on his behalf. The Department of Trade and Commerce, with whom I have not followed up the situation, have for reasons unknown to me given us no information whatsoever in connection with the trip of the Minister of Public Works.
In respect of these other departments, I am quite unaware at this moment as to whether or not their ministers have travelled outside Canada, and as to the other information requested. Despite the fact that this was an order for return made by the authority of the house, it is quite possible that these gentlemen have been jaunting around the countryside outside Canada and, for whatever
Supply-Secretary of State reasons seem right to them, have decided they will not tell the house anything about it.

am afraid the Secretary of State and I have a somewhat different interpretation of his basic responsibility in respect of these returns. I would not argue for a moment that it is the Secretary of State's responsibility to vouch for the correctness of the information or even perhaps some of the details of the information, but I would suggest that he does have the responsibility of getting the information requested in an order for return by this house-at least some information. If we accept the argument of the Secretary of State in this connection we are rapidly coming to a situation in which nobody is responsible for collating the information and seeing that returns asked for by this house are dealt with. It is the Secretary of State's responsibility to collate this information when it is obtained and to table it in this house.
I therefore suggest that since he is the man who is going to table information of this nature, when it affects more than one department of government he certainly is the man who should see that the information is available for tabling at some point. Otherwise those of us who ask questions which are made an order for return covering more than one department are left in an almost untenable position because we would have to be questioning 20 ministers in this case as to why the information was not being made available. We would have no point of contact. We would be just as much justified in questioning the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of National Defence as in questioning the Secretary of State.
But in any event, Mr. Chairman, I suggest most strongly, first, that the Secretary of State in this particular instance-and, I would be quite sure, in other instances as well- has been responsible for an unreasonable delay between the time an order for return is passed here in the house and the time it is transmitted to the department concerned.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
In this particular case the delay was two weeks. For those who may not realize what is required of the Secretary of State, may I say this. He has a standard form which is filled in on a typewriter and which is transmitted to the department concerned. It is a very simple matter. It is not one that requires concentration or great effort. Second, I would say that the Secretary of State, once he has sent out this information, makes no attempt whatsoever to see that the information is returned within a reasonable limit. He just sits here complacently and waits until other people get around to making the information available to him. Third, I would say-as proved by this particular case-that the Secretary of State does not check the information returned to him in order to make sure that the interested departments have replied. Fourth, arising from this entire situation, we have specifically here a case where the Secretary of State has tabled a return which is incomplete and in which-and there can be no argument about this one whatsoever-he has been asked for information concerning all government departments. He has tabled a return containing information from only 12 government departments. He has tabled that on his own authority and therefore, obviously, he has given the House of Commons less information than that which was asked. I have already pointed out that in at least one case among the missing departments information should have been forthcoming and that therefore the Secretary of State, had he pressed for a nil return in these cases, would have procured the information requested by the House of Commons.
Without going into detail at all, Mr. Chairman, and because I realize it is not the responsibility of the Secretary of State, I would just say that in many cases in this particular return the information which he has tabled has been factually unsatisfactory and very definitely not an answer to the questions asked in the return. It is his view-with which I do not agree-that he has no responsibility to see that the information which he tabled is at least reasonably coherent in the light of the questions asked. He feels that that is someone else's responsibility. I suggest that for the proper order of the business of the House of Commons, since the Secretary of State is the individual responsible for collating and channelling this information, it is not too unreasonable to ask that he might see that the questions asked are also answered in the information which he tables for the house.
In summation, Mr. Chairman, having set forth the deficiencies in respect of this department and its work on orders for returns, I would say that this is an extremely serious

situation. Orders tor returns are not made by one party or by one individual. They are a request for information on behalf of the entire house. Under this information, believing it to be dependable, true and complete, many of us are prepared to base statements and speeches, and do so. When we find a situation in which the information is not forthcoming for three and a half months, we are handicapped. When we are left in the position that the information tabled is incomplete, we are handicapped. When we are left in the position that the information, even if ostensibly complete, is not that requested, we are handicapped. I think that the Secretary of State could do a great deal to improve the business of this house and to supply us with the information we wanted if he would do his job properly and conscientiously instead of in the slap-happy manner that has been evidenced in this particular case.

speechtext:
I am
not too much surprised at the tone which my hon. friend has chosen to adopt in his remarks. We are constantly hearing him make criticism, sometimes for the sake of criticism. I did not want to interrupt him during his remarks but I felt that this whole speech of his was out of order because it does not concern the administration of my department. The only responsibility that the Secretary of State has is to see to it that, when they are ready, returns are tabled supplying answers given by each department. He is charged with a special responsibility of course when a question concerns a department or agency for which he is responsible to the House of Commons. I might possibly quote here a passage from Bourinot, fourth edition, which explains the duties of the Secretary of State in that regard. This reference will be found at page 248 of the fourth edition of Bourinot:
Returns in Answer.-As soon as these addresses and orders have been passed by the house, they are engrossed and forwarded immediately by the Clerk of the house to the Secretary of State, who will send them to the proper department or officer for the necessary answer.
This job has been done by a very reliable officer of my department who has done it for the last 20 years and against whom there was never any criticism voiced at any time, according to my information. Bourinot goes on to say this:
When the department or person, whose duty it is to furnish the information, has prepared it, he will return it to the Secretary of State, who will take the earliest opportunity of laying it before parliament through the medium of a minister of the crown. It is the practice for each minister in the House of Commons to present the returns relative to his own department.
In my opinion this criticism voiced by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace and

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I would not want to let this opportunity pass without commending the trade marks office staff.
I know that my hon. friend has referred to


this question in order to be helpful, but one must bear in mind that it was only last year the new Trade Marks Act came into force. During the past year there has been a great rush of applications. Certain applications, such as assignments, had to be filed before June 1 of this year, so I do not think the trade marks office could be expected to increase the staff just for the original rush. Under the circumstances, I feel that the service has been fairly good. The big difficulty, in so far as staff is concerned, is that personnel cannot be trained overnight. As one who practises before that office, I am confident that, if the directives of the officers in charge of the trade marks office are followed after the act has been in force for some time, the public at large will be satisfied.
At this time I should like to ask the Secretary of State if he has anything to report on the royal commission on patents, trade marks and copyrights. I am sorry somebody could not print them and make them available more cheaply. They are very costly in their present form. Recently I had an interview with Chief Justice Ilsley and the members of the commission. I may say that the commission is not of the view that a preliminary report should be made. Patent and copyright office-
424.	Administration division, $131,335.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this brings us to the patent and copyright office, and I have some questions to ask the minister in regard to this particular office.
The patent office is, of course, by far the largest of the three branches which include the patent, copyright and trade marks offices. It also is by far the largest revenue producer, as well as the one that presents the most work to the staff concerned.
The hon. member for Ottawa East has asked some questions about the royal commission, and the minister has indicated that we cannot look for a report from it for probably another year. That may be disappointing news to hon. members; at the same time we must recognize that this is a large field and, knowing the chairman as we do, I have no doubt the commission will undertake its task thoroughly.
However, I should like to go back to the same points in relation to the patent and copyright branch as I raised in connection with the trade marks office. I refer to the question of service to the public. Here we are dealing with branches that do charge fees to the public, and raise substantial revenues from that source. Therefore those who have business to do with these offices are entitled to as prompt and effective service as it is reasonable to expect.
Turning to the subject of revenues, I find in the last available annual report of the
Supply-Secretary of State department that, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, the receipts in round figures totalled $869,000, of which sum $848,000 was yielded by the patents branch and $21,000 from the copyright and industrial designs branch.
In the first place I would ask the minister to give us comparable figures for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955, after which I shall go on to make further comments with respect to the matter of surpluses and deficits.
Page 19 of the annual report indicates that this particular office yielded surpluses to the consolidated revenue fund in the first six years of the 10-year period there reviewed. Those surpluses ran up as high as $319,000 in the fiscal year 1947-48. However, in the last four of this 10-year period, commencing with 1950-51 and ending with 1953-54, the branch in each year has shown a deficit. So my second question is; What was the result of operations in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955? Was it a surplus or a deficit? May I just add that this era of deficits, which began in 1950-51, almost coincided with the commencement of the printing of the patents. It had begun only a short time before that, and no doubt it has entered into the expenditures of the department, and has had not a little to do with turning the annual surplus position into one of a deficit. However, we shall await the minister's answer on that point.
I turn now to the question of service. Hon. members who were in the house in 1947, particularly those who served on the banking and commerce committee of that year, will recall the extended review of the operations in the patent office conducted by that committee. At that time the backlog for patents was very substantial. The commissioner of patents of that time was complaining that his appropriations and authority did not permit him to recruit the staff he needed to give the puolic the service to which it was entitled, and he pointed out that he was sorely hampered as well by lack of accommodation.
Hon. members will recall the extended discussion which took place at that time in the house and the committee. Naturally those of us who took part in that discussion, and others since, are interested in knowing what the subsequent trend has been in these important factors which have a bearing upon the service this office is in a position to give to the public.
First of all there is the question of delays. I am sure the minister will agree with me that while the process of patenting is never one characterized by break-neck speed in any jurisdiction, nevertheless there is a limit to be tolerated by the public who are paying

Supply-Secretary of State substantial fees to the office. The report of the office as incorporated in the minister's report for the year does not set forth the number of cases in the backlog. I suggest this is proper information for us to seek from him now. So that we may test the progress the department is making in coping with the backlog, I think the minister should tell the committee about the backlog of applications on file, at all stages of processing in, let us say, the last five years. Then we shall be in a position to judge whether the backlog is growing or being reduced.
If one refers to page 17 of the minister's annual report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, one sees figures that suggest that the backlog, far from being reduced, is actually increasing. I am not saying that the figures on this table are conclusive on the subject of the backlog; the table is not set up to show the backlog at a glance. Nevertheless these are relevant figures I have drawn from the table to which I have referred. In the fiscal year 1953-54 applications for patents totalled 18,565. Some few were disposed of in other ways. But we see that the applications reported in the same fiscal year aggregated 14,524. Applications allowed aggregated 10,016, and patents issued totalled 9,405.
As I say, these figures are not set up in the table with a view to indicating a backlog. Nevertheless, there is enough of relevancy in the figures to suggest that the backlog, instead of being reduced, is actually increasing.
I am not unmindful of the fact, as drawn from this table, that the volume of applications being handled by the department is increasing. I presume the minister will be able to give us the number of applications received in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955. The total for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, was, I believe, an all-time record. That figure of 18,565 to which I have drawn attention is 2,000 more than in any previous year. I wish to be fair about this. We are not unmindful-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That record has been broken this year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I am not surprised at that. In fairness, I am not unmindful of the fact that the volume of work falling on the patent office is growing. I would ask the minister whether he will give us the backlog of applications in all stages of processing for say the last five years. I presume he has the figure at the end of the fiscal year in each case. That will enable us to judge the progress that is being made in dealing with that backlog.
Also bearing on that matter of backlog is the question of how many applications have

been allowed to remain in some stages of processing. I hope the minister will be able to give us some information as to the number of years that some of the applications-
I am thinking now of the maximum period-have been pending before the department sc that we may judge as to whether provision adequate to ensure service to the public is being made.
Now, sir, bearing on the question of delay on the one hand, or service to the public on the other, there are, I suppose, two questions. One is the question of staff; the other the question of accommodation. These are both questions that engaged the interest and the very active concern of the banking and commerce committee in 1947. We know that following those hearings some provision was made for an increase in office accommodation. Since that time there have been some increases in the staff of the department, the technical staff as well as the clerical staff. But I shall be mistaken, Mr. Chairman, if the increases in technical staff particularly have kept pace with the increase in the volume of business with which the branch is dealing.
I hope the minister will give us an adequate statement with regard to steps that have been taken to supply the branch with the accommodation it requires, both office accommodation and also storage accommodation; and second, what steps are being taken to ensure that there will be adequate staff available, both technical and clerical.
Sir, it is not always that one emphasizes the necessity of what might sometimes amount to increases in staff, but here we are dealing with offices that produce a revenue

in this case, a quite substantial revenue-paid by those who are doing business with this office and are accordingly entitled to service from it. Therefore, I hope the minister will be in a position to give the committee the rather extensive information for which I have asked.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Before the
Secretary of State answers I should like to say how pleased I am at the different attitude which has been taken in the past few years by the house with regard to the patent office. I think it is time the people realized that the patent office is not primarily a revenue-producing branch. It should not be a revenue-producing branch. It should be a service to the public.
The great difficulty with our patent system in Canada today is this. We have a very complicated Patent Act, and a very good one, Mr. Chairman. It is almost a duplicate of what exists in the United States. Parts of it are taken from the British system where they provide an extensive service at the cost of

the public. The United States patent office is not a revenue-producing system; it is a very costly office.
In this country, as I have said, we have been trying to promote a patent act which would require extensive offices and services such as exist in Great Britain and in the United States. Until the public and parliament realize that this is a costly business and that it should be carried on, I do not think we shall cure some of the evils which necessarily go along with the patent system in Canada. Of course, I understand that these are the type of things that the royal commission is inquiring into. But I want to bring to the attention of the committee once again the fact that we have a complicated patent act in this country. To put it into proper practice would require an extensive office such as exists in the United States and in Great Britain and we cannot have that until parliament is willing to pay the shot for that office.
At the present time we have delays in that office. They are owing to the fact that we have not provided the patent office with a sufficiently extensive staff to get results. In the United States, for example, the examiner is not supposed to pass upon one or two applications a day. They would never pass upon 10,000 or 12,000 applications in a year with the small staff of examiners we have here. In the United States the examiners pass one case probably every three days.
There is another angle to the United States system. The inventors realize, and the patent office insists upon, the fact that trained people should prepare patent applications. It is a technical matter. We have not insisted too much in the past upon the people hiring technical men to prepare their applications. Many of the delays in the patent office are owing to the fact that patent applications are not properly prepared and also owing to the fact that people take as long as possible to answer reports from the patent office within the delays allowed. Therefore, I hope that when the Secretary of State answers some of these questions he will say that in the future he intends-perhaps it would have to wait until the commission has reported-to put boldly before parliament the fact that if we want service in this country in the patent office we must not look at what is the revenue from the public but that we are going to pay the actual cost of providing that service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
In the first place, I should like to answer a few of the questions asked by the hon. member for Eglinton. He has dealt with the revenue position. He asked for the revenues for the year 1954-55. The revenue from patents, trade marks and copyrights totalled the sum of $1,329,631.71.
Supply-Secretary of State

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Excuse me. Can the minister give the figures for the purpose of comparison of patents and copyrights, not including trade marks? The figures that I was dealing with were of patents and copyrights alone. I was referring to pages 19 and 20 of his last previous annual report.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The breakdown for patents is $1,107,296.73 as against $869,055.08 for 195354. It is expected that there will be a surplus this year of $2,594 from the patent and copyright office, which is the first surplus in the last four or five years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
That is right. The hon. member also referred to the delays in obtaining patents which are complained about by the public, but I think he himself gave the answer. It is extremely difficult to obtain the services of qualified examiners who must be graduate engineers. During the last year this recruiting did not produce very good results as the number of examiners which the department succeeded in obtaining was less than the preceding year. The result is that the backlog to which my hon. friend referred increased this year and has now reached over 60,000. Great efforts are being made to reduce this as much as possible by obtaining the services of examiners. I may say I am informed that a delay of three and a half years is what the public must also expect in the United States.
The hon. member for Ottawa East suggested that this service should be given to the public and that the department should not operate on a revenue basis, but I do not know that that would be a sound proposal. The conditions as to recruiting are about the same in Canada as in the United States. I am informed that that country finds it extremely difficult to get examiners of patents. I do not know that I have on hand the other information requested by my hon. friend but I shall try to secure it and give it to him later.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The remaining supplementary items apply to the patent and copyright office and perhaps we could dispose of those, then adjourn and go on with other branches of this department after lunch.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I have one or two observations to make on the statement just made by the Secretary of State. I understand that he is going to obtain some of the further information I asked for and perhaps he might be able to provide this when we come back at 2.30 p.m. I asked for the backlog at the

Supply-Secretary of State end of each of the last five years and I asked also the number of years that some of these applications have been pending. I wish to know the maximum period that some of these have actually been pending.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: My hon. friend will understand that that information as to the backlog is not available for each year. It might take more than a few hours to obtain it, but I shall be pleased to get it and send it to my hon friend if it is of interest.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I have some further comments which will take but a moment or two.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
If we are going to continue to meet after ten o'clock surely we are not going through now to 2:30 p.m. There are other members of the committee who have some questions to ask.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: On Department of Secretary of State, item 424.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before recess the hon. member for Eglinton asked me a few questions to which I have not yet given complete answers. He was asking the number of applications filed. For the current fiscal year the total number is 19,446, which, of course, is an increase over the preceding year. He also asked about the pending cases in the patent office. The pending cases for the year 1952-53, to April 1 of that year, totalled 58,852. This figure increased to 63,558 for the year 1953-54. For the current year it has reached the figure of 69,616.
I might say that all these pending cases cannot be considered as cases that are not being actually processed. Out of that figure there are at least 20,000 which cannot be considered as backlog. They are cases that are actually being processed by the patent office. As I said before, it has been extremely difficult to recruit personnel for the office. I might inform the committee that there is an open competition organized by the civil service commission which tries to recruit personnel. This open competition lasts from November till September of each year. To give an example to the committee of how difficult it is to recruit engineers as patent examiners, I may say that about six weeks ago the commission advertised in about 200 Canadian newspapers to try to recruit qualified engineers.
As a result of this advertising 92 inquiries were made, and only two applications were

actually filed. They are now being examined by the civil service commission. It is quite disappointing to find that, although advertising was done throughout Canada, an unsatisfactory result was achieved and that only two applications were actually received out of a total number of 92 who inquired about the competition. Not only here in Canada but also in the United States and the United Kingdom, the same difficulties arise in so far as recruitment of personnel is concerned.
This is one of the main reasons why there is quite a delay before the applications are processed and before the actual patents are issued. The normal delay should be about two years. It is not expected that in any competent patent office an application could be processed under that minimum of two years. Actually the period is three and a half years, but it is expected that with additional efforts another group of qualified examiners may be obtained, which would relieve the situation considerably.
The hon. member for Eglinton might be interested in having this information about space, to which he alluded during his remarks. Actually the patent office is in need of space, but it is expected that by the beginning of October the moving of a unit of the printing bureau to the new printing office in Hull will make available for the patent office space of about 7,000 square feet which, it is felt by the division, will be enough to suit the needs for the current year at least.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some of these figures that the minister has given, I am sure, contain some very startling information. When I indicated that I thought we would find that the backlog of applications had risen in recent years, I had no thought whatever that we would find that the backlog had risen to these very large figures. In 1947, when the banking and commerce committee was reviewing this whole problem, including the problem of the backlog, the volume of the backlog at that time, as I recall it, stood at approximately
28,000	cases. That means that in these intervening eight years the backlog has increased to 70,000 in round figures.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt, but I am informed that the figure to which my hon. friend has just referred of some 28,000 as a backlog for the year 1947 is actually incorrect. In fact, it referred only to cases that had not been processed. The actual figure of the backlog at that time was about 45,000, I am told.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: To refer to that case in which an application has been on the files of the department for over 20 years I do not think justifies the conclusion which my hon. friend has arrived at, because it is a special case. It would be unfair simply to say that there could be a number of cases that would present the same circumstances. In fact out of the number I have mentioned of 69,616, 13,685 are over 2J years on the files.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Over what?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Supply-Secretary of State young engineers as soon as they graduate. However, it is hoped that some progress will be made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I think the minister was not following what I was saying, Mr. Chairman. When he broke in on me I was saying that I am not going to draw inferences from one fact or facts with regard to one application because, with regard to each of these longstanding applications there may be some particular circumstances that help to explain that long delay. I quite recognize the fact that we must judge by the whole picture the reasonableness of the length of time required to process. I was hoping that the minister might be able to give us the number of applications that have been pending for, say, more than five years. That would be not unreasonable. I have carefully noted his statement that 3j years is the average. I have made my comment on that matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: So far as applications are concerned that were filed prior to January, 1951, there are 1,087.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I was interested in the discussion with regard to salaries for these patent examiners. Will the minister indicate the qualifications needed? These salaries would appear to me to be extremely low having regard to the type of work required. A short time ago we were discussing the estimates of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and I referred to a geolpgist, a friend of mine, who had been in that department for 20 years but who left the department to go with the Shell Oil Company at double the salary. He had about 20 years' service in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys but he started in with the Shell Oil Company at double the salary he was receiving in the government service. If we are going to obtain people to do this work, it would appear to me that they must be paid salaries in line with those paid by private industry. Will the minister indicate what qualifications he requires of a grade 1 examiner?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The only qualification-and it is the difficult one, I suppose, to obtain-is that the applicant must be a graduate engineer from a recognized university. That is the only qualification. He receives his training in the patent office. If he is a qualified graduate engineer he may enter the service and then he receives his training there. But it just so happens that amongst those who are graduate engineers, as I said before, only 92 inquiries were made about that competition. Out of those only two made application to enter the service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: In reading the debate in 1947 and the discussion that took place in the banking and commerce committee at that time, I find that the commissioner outlined three or four things that he thought would make for improvement of the situation existing at that time. He had about 27 examiners and he thought that if he had 50 he would overtake the backlog. He now has 107. His complaint also at that time was that he did not have sufficient office space or room. He said he thought that if he had 50,000 square feet the accommodation would be ample to process the patents going through. We just had the information from the minister this afternoon that 7,000 extra square feet were obtained this year. What is the total office accommodation as to the number of square feet now?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The total is 42,000 square feet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It is still a great deal short of what the commissioner asked for at that particular time and he would probably need much more now. He outlined the difficulty he had in obtaining recruits and their training for the office. In the details here I note that where you had 50 patent examiners, grade 1, last year you are down to 42 this year. Then in the next grade, grade 2, you had 15 last year whereas you have 28 this year. That makes a sum total of 70 as compared with 65 in those two groups last year. For instance, you have either promoted them up to grades 3 and 4 or you have 30 in the classification that you call grade 3 and grade 4. The whole story is revealed here in what you call class 5. Last year you had 14 patent examiners in this grade, and today you have only seven, and you are making provision for salaries at $7,200. The complaint of the commissioner in 1947 was that he had difficulty in obtaining patent examiners because they could not find accommodation to live in Ottawa. Of course that was under war conditions. Here you have a situation where you have trained examiners who reach grade 5, and the salary is $7,200. You only have seven of that grade remaining. Where have the others gone? Is it because the salary is not sufficient to retain them?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It is the result of the classification of some of these positions. As the hon. gentleman will see, the civil service commission reclassified some of these positions from grade 4 to grade 5.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I can see that there are promotions taking place, but when you get near the top bracket or grade 5 you find that last year you had 14 and this year you only have seven. They have not been promoted to

grade 6, because if you revert to the previous page you find that you have only one grade 6 patent examiner and you have none in grade 7, whereas you had one last year. You seem to have lost your best man.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: This is dealt with by the civil service commission, and is the result of the yearly reclassification that they make. I think that amongst the 20 patent examiners you have there, you will find some whose maximum salary is the same as the minimum salary for grade 5.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am not trying to hamper or criticize, but rather to point out that what the commissioner was complaining about in 1947 is continuing. You are not providing sufficient salary to retain your competent men. After you bring them to the top, evidently $7,200 is not going to be enough to retain these men. According to these figures you have lost seven of your top men.

427. To provide for special expenditure in connection with a commission under the Inquiries Act to inquire into the working of the Patent Act, the Copyright Act, the Industrial Designs Act and other related legislation, $35,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

The order of reference does affect any matter that falls within the legislation to which the hon. member has referred. For instance, it deals with incentive; if there is sufficient incentive for the public to have the full benefit of the legislation, and that would be an item that would cover the subject referred to by the hon. member.
Supply-Secretary of State

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am not quite clear yet, if the minister will be patient with me. Will he be a little more explicit as to just what the royal commission is doing? maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I will read the order of reference as it appears in the order in council:
Establishing a commission of inquiry under the authority of part I of the Inquiries Act, to inquire as to whether federal legislation relating in any way to patents of invention, industrial designs, copyright and trade marks affords reasonable incentives to invention and research, to the development of literary and artistic talent, to creativeness, and to making available to the Canadian public scientific, technical, literary and artistic creations and their applications, adaptations and uses, in a manner and on terms adequately safeguarding the paramount public interest, the whole in the light of present-day economic conditions, scientific, technical and industrial developments, trade practices and any other relevant factors or circumstances, including practices under or related to the said legislation and any relevant international convention to which Canada is a party; to submit to the governor in council a report on its findings, with any recommendations that may appear to it advisable for changes in the said legislation.
I think if we refer to those terms we shall find that the things the hon. gentleman has mentioned may be relevant factors that could be dealt with by the commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I would appreciate it if the minister would give the committee a detailed exposition as to the authority and the policy of administration of the civil service commission, as it relates to all civil servants of the federal government. All the ministers are in charge of their departments, and in those departments they have hundreds of thousands of employees. The salaries for those employees are set out in the estimates of each department.
Do I take it that there is some form of over-all control by the civil service commission? How far does the administration and authority of the commission go in the matter of hours of work, wages, overtime rates of pay, regular rates of pay and the like, so far as civil servants are concerned? That information along general lines would be welcomed by hon. members, I am sure.
But I should like to bring this discussion to a more particularized basis. I am told that when a person is taken on the strength of the protective security staff in the House of Commons he is taken on as a temporary employee. However, after having served for five sessions, I believe it is, he goes on a permanent basis. I presume there must be some jurisdiction and authority by the civil service commission over this staff, because they are civil servants.
I would appreciate it if the minister would inform us as to whether or not any serious consideration is being given to placing the protective security staff at all times throughout the year on a 40-hour week. I know that nominally they are supposed to work a 40-hour week, but when the house is in
Supply-Secretary of State session they cannot follow that regulation. And when we have a situation such as we have had in the last seven weeks, when the house has been meeting at eleven o'clock in the morning, and sitting through until ten o'clock, or later, in the evening, it would seem that these men are putting in at least four hours of overtime each day. Already they have accumulated 112 hours of overtime. I do not think it is right when the house is sitting for a period of approximately seven months. I think it is going to increase as the years go by; for as the population of Canada increases the work of the House of Commons will increase. Why should a condition be allowed to continue under which these men as civil servants are not entitled to, or are not receiving in fact, the same rights and hours of work a week as the majority of the civil servants in Canada, and as the majority of the employees in private concerns in Canada?
As I say, these men now have approximately 112 hours of overtime at this session. How are they to be paid for that overtime? I was interested, and I asked them that question and they said: "We do not know and we cannot find out." Are they to be paid in cash, or are they going to have time off? Personally, I think they would prefer the money; personally, I think they ought to get the money. They ought to know, after they have worked 112 hours overtime, whether they are going to get their money or their time off. If they are going to get time off, is it going to be on a decent and responsible basis so that they can plan ahead and take advantage of the 112 hours, or is it to be at the whim and will of the government as to when they can take the time off? It is a most unfortunate situation that employees of the government, in this case, the employees of the House of Commons, who are actually here at the service of the House of Commons and the Senate, should be in the position in which they find themselves at the present time. Therefore, I sincerely hope that the Secretary of State will give us the general picture of the power or the authority of the administration or of the civil service commission. In particular, will he tell us whether or not they are going ahead with some definite plan to employ the additional three or four men who are required so as to guarantee all through the year that the protective staff have the 40-hour week?
Second, are these men going to be paid for the 112 hours they have already put in, the money that is their due, or is some definite and decent arrangement to be made so that these men can have the time off?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for what he has said. I appreciate the remarks

Supply-Secretary of State he has made about the protective staff of the House of Commons and the Senate. This is a matter which surely affects also the privileges of this house and of the other place. I suppose they are matters that must also be studied by both Speakers of the two places. The problem has been raised. I am grateful to the hon. member for having brought it up. I have great sympathy for the men whose position he has explained.
I am informed that the men are generally paid on a days-off basis instead of getting extra salary for the extra work. In any event, I shall be pleased to bring this matter to the attention of the Speakers of both places and of the commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Has the commission any
authority at all over this matter?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It has authority if it receives requests from the House of Commons or from the Senate; otherwise it is not within the authority of the commission to intervene.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Has it any authority to receive a request from the employees to interest itself in the matter?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am sure it has to be channelled through the Speakers of the two places. The requests have to be made through the Speakers of the two places.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I should now like to deal with a different matter. It must come under this item because it has to do with civil service insurance. I presume civil service insurance comes under the civil service commission?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That would be the finance department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Fine; I shall raise it there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I wish to ask the Secretary of State a few questions. Can he explain to the house what is the procedure in procuring personnel for various departments? First of all, who decides that a certain position is necessary? How is it done? How do they proceed to procure persons suitable to fill the positions? How long does it usually take after a department requests that a certain position be filled before that position is filled by the civil service commission?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The information is along these lines. The deputy minister of each department decides whether a new employee is needed or an additional position is necessary in the department. He so informs the civil service commission. Then it does have to receive the approval of treasury board. After it has been approved by treasury board the civil service commission is informed and then a competition is organized and advertised. The selection is then made by the civil

service commission. So far as delays are concerned, it depends on the nature of the position and the difficulty of recruiting the proper person required for the job.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Does the situation ever arise where a deputy minister says that he requires a certain employee in his department and the civil service commission say, "We do not think you require this employee" and do not supply the person?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes, it does happen.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Yesterday when the estimates of the Department of Labour were before us I suggested to the acting minister that an investigation should be made into the civil service commission in connection with the administration of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. I have in my hand one of the many circulars that have been distributed recently in connection with positions. It says:
Married women may apply, but will be listed for temporary appointment only unless they can satisfy the commission that they are required to be self-supporting. An affidavit to this effect must accompany the application.
I should like the minister to explain in more detail just how it is decided that married women may apply for employment if they are required to be self-supporting? It seems to me that this is based on the assumption that Canada has just a very limited piece of pie available, and cannot make a larger pie. When my wife and I were first married she used to make quite small pies, but big enough for the two of us. But as the children came along she obtained larger pie plates and made larger pies and more pies. This has interest to me. If married women want to work they should not be prevented from working. If any department decides that a married woman is incapable, then they should have the right to fire her. Certainly, in this day and age, there should be no discrimination on the basis of one's marital status. Can the minister explain why we have the regulation? How do you determine whether a woman requires work to be self-supporting?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I might inform my hon. friend that this situation is under review at the moment. Possibly there may be a change, but it is under study.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: My criticism is that it has been decided. Here is government policy. When did it become government policy?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That has been the past practice, but it is now being reviewed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It has been the policy since when?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Since 1939.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It was never changed during the war?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes, it was changed during the war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: If it was changed during the war, that is what I am complaining about. Who was responsible for making the change during the war? It was decided that for the sake of the common good married women should be encouraged to work. I submit that in peacetime the more people who work the more work there will be and the higher the standard of living will be for all the Canadian people. Who had the responsibility for making the decision that married women cannot get jobs unless-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: During the war, for obvious reasons.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Has an order in council been passed? Who has been responsible for making this change?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: An order in council was passed to revert to the former position.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Will the minister table the order in council?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I will.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I think this is the proper time once again to register a protest that not all civil servants in Canada employed by this government are being given the benefit of the five-day 40-hour week. We have uttered this protest on other occasions. It must be done continuously until the day comes when this government will not only consider itself as an average employer in the community in which it operates but will make up its mind to be a model employer in all the communities across Canada. I fail to see any equity in the position of one civil servant having to work a 44-hour week while another civil servant doing exactly the same type of work is required to work only a 40-hour week simply because he happens to live in a different area. I realize it would mean an increase in the cost of operating government but it is an increase which all organized labour would heartily endorse and the people would be glad to pay for. We should like to see the government of Canada lead the way in providing adequate working conditions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
As my hon. friend no doubt knows, about 90 per cent of the civil service are now on the five-day, 40-hour week basis. The policy of the government is to increase gradually the number when industrial conditions are such that an increase is justified.
Supply-Secretary of State

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Is a new policy being announced by the minister when he says that they are gradually increasing the number? Is it the intention of the government to eventually have all civil servants on a five-day week?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That has been the practice, to gradually increase the number when industrial conditions in a given locality justify it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The minister has just said that the government follows the practice of paying the wages paid by industry in the area and I should like to direct the minister's attention to a condition which exists in my constituency. The customs and immigration employees in part of the area are on a five-day week while those in another part are not. I took up this matter and the explanation given was that industry in part of the area was not on a 40-hour week. I know that area as well as anyone in the department, and whoever is giving that information to the civil service commission is not giving correct information.
Industry in the area consists of lumbering, railroading, hydroelectric and things like that and there is no justification for this discrimination. The civil service commission must have got some information which is not correct. I complained earlier but was put off with the statement that this was going to go through. The point is that for months customs and immigration officers have been discriminated against and I submit that that is wrong. There must be something wrong with the information coming to the commission because there is no justification for this treatment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There is no special method by which the commission obtains its information and any information coming to the commission is dealt with. The practice is for these requests to go to the commission through the unemployment insurance commission. If my hon. friend wishes to supply me with full information I will be glad to take it up with the civil service commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Can the Secretary of State tell me whether the civil servants in the Trail area are working the same number of hours per week as the employees of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I shall have to look into the matter and supply the information later.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I think it would bear
investigation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Is the civil service commission responsible for setting the wage rates and working conditions of casual employees?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Why is not the prevailing rate principle applied to casual employees? If I might give one example, in the evidence given in the industrial relations committee with respect to casual employees of the unemployment insurance commission, it was indicated that the same rate was paid right across the country, regardless of what prevailing rate might exist in a certain area. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just wish to make a short preliminary statement with reference to this division of the department's activities. The estimates we are submitting cover the operation of the customs and excise divisions

of the Department of National Revenue, consisting of the headquarters branches at Ottawa, their field officers and some 271 ports, 25 outports and 130 out-offices situated throughout the country.
This division was responsible for the collection of revenue amounting to over $1,449 million in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1955. As the house is aware, the greatest part of this revenue is derived through the control of imported goods, the collection of customs duties, excise and sales taxes, excise duties on alcohol and tobacco products, as well as revenue derived from seizures, penalties, etc.
I think the house will agree with me that in this division, which is responsible for raising so large a part of the revenue upon which the whole framework of government is supported, any arbitrary reduction of staff or money could result in inadequate customs and excise examination and supervision with attendant loss of revenue to the crown, and would indeed be false economy.
Whilst there is a decrease of $204,850 in vote 289, construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, over last year, there is an over-all increase in the estimates of $931,741. The greatest part of this is accounted for by salaries and wages, the remainder being made up of such things as living allowances, commissionaire service, travelling expenses, rental accommodation, cartage, repairs and upkeep of buildings and works, etc.
With this short preliminary statement, I think we can proceed to a more detailed examination of the different items. I shall be very happy to answer any questions which come along.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have every intention of following the minister's admirable example of being very brief. I should like to ask him one or two general questions first. There was a time a few years ago when the customs and excise department had work to do for other departments on such matters as foreign exchange, import quotas and that kind of thing. Do those duties still exist, or have they mainly come to an end?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the ones that we took on during the war have, but we still have partial administration of something like 40 other different acts.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

I turn to another matter. My attention was drawn to what apparently is a

practice in the department with the publication last month of order in council P.C. 1955935, dated June 23, 1955. This is an order in council containing regulations governing payments for assistance in respect of offences against the customs laws and the Excise Act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this has been a practice for a great many years, I think almost since confederation. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

Supply-National Revenue

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What is the situation with regard to diplomatic clearances, the goods of diplomats coming in? What happens to their effects?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Goods brought in by diplomats are admitted free of customs duties and taxes and without examination; that is diplomatic immunity. This refers to all countries. Our people, when they go to foreign countries, are given exactly the same privilege.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister has already answered my next question. Our own people returning get the same privilege?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Supposing a Canadian diplomat goes to the United States or Europe, the same privileges are given to him as we give to representatives of those countries coming into Canada. They pay no customs duties or taxes on the goods that they bring in. There is one exception to that, and that is automobiles. If an automobile were purchased by a diplomat he gets that immunity provided the automobile is not sold within a period of two years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Do our own returning members of the external affairs department get any concession with their effects which they may accumulate abroad?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes. People returning to this country get an exemption from taxation provided that they have been away from the country a year or over, and provided the goods have been in their possession for a period of six months. They cannot dispose of these goods within a period of 12 months, otherwise they would have to pay tax. This applies not only to diplomats but to Canadian citizens coming back to their own country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What is the situation with regard to premises occupied under lease by the Department of National Revenue? Is the rental paid by the department or by the Department of Public Works?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

speechtext: How much out of this item of $130,000 for law and other costs has been set up for this particular use?

speechtext: Well, the experience has been that the amount paid is so small there is no specific amount set up for it. It is included in this amount. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Could the minister say whether any special exemptions are given to members of the armed forces with respect to the amount of goods they may bring into this country after being stationed abroad?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I want to ask the minister regarding a principle which one finds in several sections of the act. I refer to section 132 which says that any officer, having first made an oath before a justice of the peace that he has reasonable cause to suspect that goods liable to forfeiture-and so on-may enter. Now, that is an officer of the national revenue department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: An officer of the customs and excise division.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I wish the minister would say a word as to the operation of that power which his official has, just as if he were an officer of a police force. I do not want to dwell on it particularly, but I want to know whether it operates smoothly or whether it runs us into difficulties?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We have no trouble in that particular regard. I am told that it is usually done on the basis of a writ, so that gives the authority. Under the definition in the Customs Act an officer means a person employed in the administration or enforcement of the act, and this includes a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. They act as our officers in a great many instances.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I am very interested in what the minister said. You do, in fact,

usually avail yourselves of a writ. In other words, you do not rely wholly on this section?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: In the event of an emergency, when it is not possible to obtain a writ, the officer has authority under this section to act in that capacity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Has the department given consideration to some other approach to the collection of duties on very small purchases? For instance, I have before me one where the purchase was only a matter of several dollars and the collection of duty yielded only a dollar or two. Obviously in those cases, if one attempted to isolate the cost of collection, it does not pay. On the other hand, I quite appreciate that there must be one rule applicable to all. Has any consideration been given, apart from the existing exemptions in relation to purchases by persons who have been in the United States for 48 hours and are bringing goods back in their baggage, to exemption in those cases of small purchases where it obviously is not worth while for the department to attempt to collect the very small amount of duty involved?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We are an administrative department entirely. We have not that authority. If the law said that there would be exemptions up to $5 or so, we would do that. We have an arrangement working in some places whereby we make it easier for the ordinary citizen who has an invoice for a book or something of that sort, and which goes to the customs postal branch. In the city of Montreal, for instance, instead of having that person go down to the customs office and pay his tax, we have made arrangement with the postal authorities whereby the tax is collected at his home. This is experimental within the last two or three years, and we hope that in due time it may be extended to many more places.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Would there be any serious administrative difficulty involved? I can appreciate that perhaps this problem might fall on the shoulders of the Minister of Finance rather than those of the Minister of National Revenue. But is there any serious administrative problem involved if some exemption in the case of small purchases were introduced?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No, it would make it that much easier for us in the handling of a lot of small parcels. It would be a convenience and I am sure it would have an effect upon the revenue because, as you know, many muckles make a mickle.

Would the minister explain the difference in responsibility between a port and an outport?
