In his duties he was fair and benevolent.
The report which was tabled in the house on June 17, and is to be found at pages 763-5 o' Votes and Proceedings, was not unanimous. There were some sections of that report which we of the Conservative party did support, but there were a number of sections in the report against which we were obliged to vote, and the report itself was a majority report. We voted against it.
I should like to say in general, sir, that I think it is opportune that even though this hour is very late and the stage of this session is very advanced, there should be even this limited opportunity for debate, because I am convinced-and I have sat on every one of these committees on broadcasting since 1945-that we are rapidly approaching a juncture where there are important changes
6842	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Revenue that are bound to be made. There are some issues that are becoming clearer, it seems to me, than ever before; the issues of freedom, of competition, of parliamentary control and some sense of restraint and responsibility in regard to the expenditure of public moneys. I am not going to be so bold as to make excessive predictions, but I shall be a very surprised person, sir, if some quite material changes in government policy do not develop within the next year or year and a half in relation to this whole question of broadcasting and television.
At the present time there are three major issues that are apparent. The first is the issue as to the separate regulatory tribunal. The second is the issue as to the government's policy of monopoly in television; and the third, and by no means least important issue, is the colossal rate at which expenditures, particularly on television, at the expense of the taxpayer are mounting up.
Now, sir, it is not unfair to say that those errors and unsound features in government policy against which we in Her Majesty's loyal opposition have been this long time warning the house are becoming more manifest now than ever; and the system has, because of the weight of its own colossal cost and the unsoundness of certain features of government policy, come to the point where some change must be made. I am convinced that some change will be made. There are other issues, but they do not rank with these three in importance.
I should like to touch briefly upon some of the highlights that stand out in connection with these three issues.
First of all in regard to the basis of regulation and control and licensing in the field of radio broadcasting and television, the official opposition sought to place its views in this respect before the committee in the form of an amendment. That amendment was defeated by a vote of 9 to 6. I would point out that in addition to the votes of the Conservative members of the committee, that particular amendment commanded the support of the Social Credit members and also of one Liberal member, the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond. That amendment sets forth the position of the Conservative party in reference to this matter of regulation, control and licensing in the field of radio and television. It reads:
It is unnecessary and unsound that C.B.C. should continue to license, regulate and control privately-owned broadcasting stations. The committee proposes that these functions should be detached from C.B.C., and should be conferred upon a separate regulatory tribunal appointed by the governor-in-council and operating in the public interest. This will leave C.B.C. free to concentrate all its efforts on its own operation of the national system of broadcasting. The separate regulatory (Mr. Fleming.]

tribunal should deal with all questions of licensing, regulation and control as applied to all forms of broadcasting, whether public or private, and whether of sound or television. This will ensure justice and fair play for all forms of broadcasting.
There are many precedents to support this proposal of an independent regulatory tribunal. The Australian broadcasting system is organized on precisely that basis. Here in Canada we have a board of transport commissioners which regulates the operations of the railways, whether publicly-owned or privately-owned. No one would suggest that the C.N.R., in addition to carrying on its own operations, should be authorized by law to regulate and control the operations of the C.P.R. and other privately-owned railways in Canada. Yet that would be the counterpart of the present system of radio broadcasting control in Canada today. Similarly, the air transport board licenses and regulates all forms of civil aviation in Canada. No one would suggest that the publicly-owned Trans-Canada Air Lines, in addition to carrying on its own operations, should have complete power to license and control all privately-owned forms of civil aviation in Canada. Yet that also would be the counterpart of our present system of radio broadcasting in Canada.
The danger of monopoly is great under any circumstances. It is particularly threatening when applied to such a vitally important medium for the dissemination of thought and opinion.
To those who say you cannot make a comparison in this regard with two transcontinental railway systems I would reply, Very well. Perhaps a comparison in the field of civil aviation is closer, because there you have a government-owned transcontinental aviation system and a privately-owned system which is not transcontinental in the sense that it is competitive with the publicly-owned system. It seems to me that there you have a fair basis of comparison. No one whom I know of in this house suggests that Trans-Canada Air Lines should be given regulatory power over Canadian Pacific Air Lines. We were told in the committee that about one-third of the time of the board and executive of the corporation is devoted to affairs pertaining to licensing, regulation and control over the privately-owned stations. We contend that if the C.B.C. is relieved of this obligation the public interest will be served, and on the other hand the C.B.C. will have a freer hand to go ahead and make a success of its operation of the national system.
On this matter of licensing I should make this comment, because it engaged the attention of the committee. In all the years the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been the body which has reviewed applications for licences-the practice is for the Department of Transport to refer every application to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for review-there has been only one instance where the Department of Transport departed from the recommendation of the corporation within recent times and that was in connection with an application from St. John's, Newfoundland.

to set up a privately-owned television station there. When the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation weighed and reviewed that application it decided that it would like to have that channel for the opening of a C.B.C. television station there, and it made that recommendation to the Department of Transport. But in that one case, described as unique by the officials of the Department of Transport, the government did not give effect to the recommendation of the C.B.C. But the fact was that the C.B.C., as the licensing review body, found itself in the position where it was weighing its own interests against the interests of a private applicant seeking to be licensed to operate a television station on that particular channel in St. John's. The case points to the fundamental duality of C.B.C. interests in the present system.
On May 19, as reported on page 3909 of Hansard, I put the following question to the Prime Minister:
May I ask the Prime Minister if the government is contemplating the appointment of a royal commission to review the basis of regulation and control of radio broadcasting in Canada?
The Prime Minister replied:
I can say to the hon. gentleman that the government is contemplating the appointment of a commission, but that does not mean that any decision about an immediate appointment has been reached.
The government should make up its mind on what it is going to do in this matter. There is general expectation that the appointment of a royal commission will be made. I think the Minister of National Revenue owes it to the committee to tell us whether that royal commission is going to be appointed. The present system under which the corporation is placed in the position of being competitor, judge, jury and executioner is not good. This set-up has not been attacked alone by the Conservative party; it has been attacked as well within the Liberal party itself. Last March the advisory council of the national Liberal federation met in Ottawa, and a Canadian Press dispatch of March 30 revealed that the federation recommended "that the government appoint a commission to consider bringing Canadian radio and television broadcasting under an independent regulatory tribunal".
That is not the first recommendation of this nature which has emanated from some organ within the Liberal party. The young Liberals have come forward with similar recommendations, and in the face of most strenuous efforts put forward by ministers of the crown in an effort to staunch this flow of liberal ideas among young Liberals. To illustrate the matter a little further, Professor Marcus Long, who is I believe a member
Supply-National Revenue of the executive of the national Liberal federation and with whose ideas I do not hold in all respects, had this to say on this very issue. I refer to a Canadian Press dispatch of March 23, which reads as follows:
Marcus Long, associate professor of philosophy at the University of Toronto, said today he would support the formation of an independent commission controlling radio and television in Canada to avoid the potential evils of government control.
The same gentleman was quoted a few days later in a Canadian Press dispatch of April 13 from Vancouver to the following effect:
Dr. Marcus Long of Toronto, one of Canada's top education authorities, said today he believes the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is defeating its own aim of achieving a high level of entertainment by its control over radio and television.
Dr. Long, professor of philosophy at the University of Toronto, said in an interview here he favors an independent regulatory commission for radio and television in this country.
Then further:
"I am opposed to any more government control than is necessary," he said. "If it is necessary to err between control and freedom, it is better to err on the side of freedom. That is, increase the number of private stations rather than increase government monopoly and control."
Mr. Long said under present controls, private stations are "getting away with murder because the C.B.C. is afraid to enforce its own regulations: afraid that it mignt look like political pressure. An independent regulatory board could do the job without suspicion."
Now, sir, there are the comments of some outstanding Liberals on this subject.
The next issue on which I should like to pass comment tonight is the government policy of monopoly in the field of television. I do not need to go back and read the history of the control of television in Canada. I attempted to do so when speaking to the house on March 8 and on occasions in earlier sessions. But it will be remembered that the first period in government policy was the period of delay, when the government would not permit anybody to develop television in Canada or to risk his money in that field. The second stage was the pre-emption by the government of the plums in the form of the channels available, one in each of the six major metropolitan areas of Canada. The third stage went along with that. Having pre-empted the plums, the policy of the government then became to impose upon all of Canada what is in effect the policy of local monopoly in television. It poses under the title of the "single service coverage policy"-a very euphonious title which masks or disguises the ugly features of monopoly.
Government policy in this field has been declared on two occasions on behalf of the

Supply-National Revenue government by the Minister of National Revenue. Those occasions were December 8, 1952, and March 30, 1953. We were told in the committee that government policy remains unchanged. There were some Liberal members of the committee who looked for the emergence of some change in government policy, but it is evident that thus far at any rate there has been no change in the government policy of aiding, abetting and imposing monopoly.
However, there is another feature of this matter that calls for comment. It is the boast of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that it follows not government policy or government dictate but parliamentary policy and parliamentary dictate. The policy of the government in relation to the imposition of a monopoly in the field of television has never been approved by the Canadian parliament. On this occasion the government had a clear course open to it. If it wanted parliamentary approval of its monopolistic policy it had an opportunity to seek it by bringing forward a motion for the adoption of the report of the committee on broadcasting, because that report in effect gave sanction to the government's monopolistic policy. But the government has carefully eschewed that.
I asked Mr. Dunton in the committee what policy the C.B.C. is applying in relation to television licensing. His answer was the policy enunciated by the minister on December 8, 1952, and March 30, 1953. I have to say in the light of the facts, therefore, that what the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been applying in these past three years has not been a policy to which parliament has given its approval. It is a government policy. The government has never once submitted its policy of monopoly in television to the test in this house.
There are very good reasons for that. Had the government done so there would have been an opportunity to divide the house and to see how far the rank and file of Liberal members of this house are prepared to give their support to this monopolistic policy. The government has carefully avoided that course. It has carefully avoided giving the house the opportunity of expressing itself.
What about the opposition?

I am about to state our policy now, as set forth in one of the amendments which we sought to write into the report but which was defeated by a vote of 9 to 6. Again let me remind the minister who just interrupted me that among the 6 who supported our amendment were Conservative and Social Credit members and a Liberal member, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. I regret

that it is so long, but here we are dealing with statements of party policy, and I think I should put the statement of the Conservative party's policy on record as it is set out here:
In establishing its own T.V. stations and dealing with applications for privately-owned T.V. stations the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been adhering to the policy announced by the government in the House of Commons on December 8, 1952, and March 30, 1953. There has been no change in the policy since. This policy of local monopoly has been clothed with the euphonious title "the single service coverage policy". C.B.C. has occupied six principal urban centres, Halifax, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Winnipeg, and Vancouver, thus from the point of view of commercial revenue picking off all the biggest plums for itself. Eighteen privately-owned, television transmitting stations are operating. They are, however, restricted to areas where no C.B.C. station is operating, and they are now given by the government's policy a complete Canadian monopoly in their local areas. To carry out this policy channels have been juggled and shifted about. The government's policy creates and protects monopoly both for the C.B.C. and for private stations. That policy is already breaking down. Overlapping is now occurring in the areas served by some stations, at least where the viewer has an outdoor antenna.
The committee condemns this policy of monopoly. It believes that Canadian competition will have a healthy effect on both C.B.C. and private stations in their operations, in their service to the listening public, and in all forms of their programming. American competition is an existing fact. Millions of Canadians are within access of television from stations located in the United States. These stations send their signals into Vancouver, Montreal, Toronto, and the populous areas of southwestern Ontario. Their programs are popular. Indeed, unchallenged evidence before the committee showed that the Buffalo stations are listened to by almost twice as many Canadians as the C.B.C. T.V. stations in Toronto. Thus the government's policy of monopoly prevents Canadian competition, but not American. The United States stations have not been slow to exploit the protected position created for them by the exclusion of all Canadian privately-owned stations from the six major urban areas. By selling time to Canadian advertisers they are taking $2 million per annum in commercial revenues out of Canada.
Mr. Dunton testified that approximately 50 per cent of all programs in the C.B.C. television system are of United States origin. Private broadcasters indicated to the committee that they would expect to offer approximately the same percentage of Canadian content in their programs if licensed to operate. This is one of the things which proper regulation and control could effectively ensure, subject always to the right of the Canadian people to enjoy programs of their democratic choosing.
The policy of local monopoly is preventing the erection of French-language stations as well as English-language stations.
The dangerous policy of monopoly cannot be justified on the argument that C.B.C. must have all the commercial revenues from the six "plum" urban areas. At the present time the C.B.C. is enjoying revenues of approximately $30 million per annum. Of this sum only $6 million comes from commercial revenues. The balance comes from the public treasury and is provided by the taxpayers. The C.B.C. is not and never has been dependent upon its commercial revenues for the extension of its broadcasting or television facilities.
It is the opinion of the committee that competition is desirable in the public interest, and that

its desirability increases with the rapid increase in the number of television sets in use in Canada. The dangers of the present policy of monopoly are thus constantly increasing.
I do not think I need to enlarge on the points made in that statement of party position. I mention the fact that the government's policy excludes Canadian competition but not United States competition. Here in my hand I hold an advertisement of a United States station advertising that its services extend to certain states of the American union and the province of Quebec. How can a policy of this kind be justified? It means that $2 million per annum is going out of Canada in the form of advertising, and it means that the system is breaking down today because of its own inherent unsoundness. There is overlapping of coverage. It cannot any longer be prevented. This is the soft of thing that led the Vancouver Sun in its leading front page editorial on March 26 to comment as follows:
The spectacle of liberalism forsaken by false friends appears in frightening aspect in Ottawa. The federal government has deserted its principles in favour of a new anti-democratic idolatry of which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is the worst symbol. The Liberal party's own traditions are mocked by the delegation of absolute power to the C.B.C. in radio and television. Thoughtful members of parliament must be sadly aware that C.B.C.'s network and big-city monopolies in radio and television are a denial of public and private rights.
That editorial also points out the benefits that competition would bring, that the absence of competition brings decay and corruption and that this is true also in politics. So I say it is evident that there must be some change, because it cannot long be postponed.
On May 19 I also asked the Prime Minister this second question:
Is the government contemplating either the abandonment or modification of the so-called policy of single station coverage with respect to television, that is to say the policy of local monopoly of television in Canada?
To that question the Prime Minister made this reply, as reported at page 3909 of Hansard:
The question is not one to which a categorical yes or no can be given. The policy has never been that there would be, for all time, only one station in each locality. The whole matter is under constant consideration, and the question as to when it will be deemed proper to declare that applications for duplication of service will be entertained is part of that consideration. It may very well be that no decision would be arrived at before the appointment of the commission to which the hon. member referred in his previous question.
If a royal commission is going to be appointed by the government to inquire into this whole field and to recommend in relation to policy, why does not the government do
Supply-National Revenue the straightforward thing and come out and announce the appointment of that royal commission? The fact of the matter is, Mr. Chairman, that C.C.F. policies have dominated the thinking of the government in this field up until now, and it is going to take some effort to shake the Liberal party thinking-that is Liberal with a capital "L"-free of the socialistic tentacles that have been fastened upon radio and television policy under the present government. I am certain there are some members of the government opposite who cannot approve this kind of policy in principle. I hope they are going to be more vocal hereafter than they have been hitherto in influencing government policy.
Mr. Chairman, in reference to radio and television there is no issue arising now that is more important than the whole question of finances. That matter, together with the question of auditing and accounting, will be dealt with by my colleague the hon. member for Perth. I just wish to make this one comment in passing on a matter in which I took some interest in the committee. It is this publication "CBC Times", a rather attractive publication that is put out at a cost of $82,500 per annum against which the C.B.C. derives revenue of $27,000, so the publication costs $55,500 net per annum to the Canadian taxpayer.
The purpose of this publication is to announce programs. But what do we find in the issue of July 28? We find the whole report-the majority report-of the committee. As if that is not enough, we find that statements in paragraph 16 of that report, selected from the evidence of Mr. Dunton, have been italicized so as to draw particular attention to them. These remarks of Mr. Dunton are not italicized in the report but are italicized in this C.B.C. publication as follows:
. . . we are perfectly convinced and think it is very plain that it is impossible for anyone or anybody to operate a nation-wide service in this country-a national service in sound and television-on a purely commercial basis.
I do not think that is a proper use to make of public funds for this publication. We were told that this substantial cost to the Canadian taxpayer was justified because this publication acquainted the public with programs of the C.B.C. Now we find that it is being used to publicize the majority report and, in particular, a statement of Mr. Dunton which is challenged in certain quarters.
Mr. Chairman, there are many matters that would justify comment, but the hour is late and I do not wish to prolong these remarks. In the committee I drew attention to the way in which the so-called policy of balance in programs of opinion and comment is not working out satisfactorily; and that what we

Supply-National Revenue find put forward in the guise of adherence to the policy of balance represents a pronounced imbalance as, for instance, Mr. Matthew Hal-ton doing practically all the programs and comment from London and Mr. LaChance those from Paris.
Here in Canada, if there were time or if the house had the patience to hear it at length, I should be glad to review the evidence put before the committee indicating the extent to which there is a failure to follow the policy of balance in the selection of those who are participating in programs of comment and opinion right here in Ottawa. There is apparently something approaching a monopoly within a monopoly. The committee- and this was perhaps quite extraordinary -went so far, in the light of those disclosures, as to give support to a Conservative amendment. This is the amendment that was adopted, if you please, by the committee and appears in the majority report:
In a medium which exerts so strong an influence on public thought as radio and television it is desirable that the greatest care be taken to provide balance and freedom in the presentation of opinion. The committee suggests this be constantly kept in view in seeking a wider selection in those participating in the programs.
There are many matters that could be reviewed, but I do not propose to detain the committee longer except to comment on one upon which there has been some degree of public misunderstanding. It is in regard to what I said on March 8, concerning free time for the communist party at election time. This was pictured in some quarters as an assertion that there should be some attempt at suppression of freedom of speech. That is, of course, a nonsensical interpretation to place on the remarks that were put before the house on that occasion, or indeed on any other occasion.
What we are dealing with here is not political broadcasting generally, but the question of free time for recognized political parties at election time. Any communist in this country who wishes to obtain time on the air to diffuse his wicked propaganda is quite at liberty to go to any radio station in this country, whether operated by the C.B.C. or any private station, and purchase time for that purpose. That is not what we are dealing with; we are dealing with the particular provision, under existing policy, recognizing the right of political parties to free radio time at election time. The position we have taken on behalf of the Conservative party is that we do not approve of giving time to communists on that basis at election time as an organized political party. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police of this

country have had something to say about this labour progressive party that is a cloak for communism.
Our position in this respect was clearly stated in an amendment we sought to introduce in the committee, which reads as follows:
The committee, while affirming the principle of freedom of expression, cannot fail to take note of the fact that the present regulations respecting political broadcasts have been used by the communists to obtain free network time at public expense for the so-called labour progressive party by the device of nominating straw candidates in general elections. The committee also notes that in the recent general election in the United Kingdom no free time was given by B.B.C. to the communist party. The committee recommends that consideration be given by the board of governors to the revision of the regulations in such a manner as to prevent their being circumvented for this purpose.
We, I think, could be satisfied in this country to follow the example of the United Kingdom. The recognition of the labour progressive party as a recognized political party is the responsibility of the C.B.C. The political parties were brought in only after that decision, to decide on the apportionment of time amongst recognized political parties. It is no responsibility of any other political party that time should have been given to the communists, free time at the taxpayers' expense.
I simply conclude with this. This system, by reason of its developed weaknesses, its inherent unsoundness, its suppression of freedom, its suppression of competition in favour of monopoly and the colossal cost to the Canadian taxpayer, as my colleague the hon. member for Perth will show, has brought us to the point now in Canada that in this house we are requesting a fundamental revision in policy in relation to radio and television broadcasting.

I did not intend to speak this evening, but after listening to the hon. member for Eglinton I cannot resist the temptation of making a few comments on what he has said. He said the government was following C.C.F. policy in regard to radio. My opinion is that the government has followed very closely the policy laid down by Right Hon. R. B. Bennett when he was prime minister of this country some years ago. Mr. Bennett pointed out to the house, when the original radio commission was set up, that if governments could do it they would like to recall the privileges they gave to the railways and so on, when the railways were established in this country. It is just as necessary to have control over the railway system, so Mr. Bennett alleged and I think properly, as it is over the radio waves. He

said the radio waves were a natural resource of the country, and they must remain under the control of the nation.
What my hon. friend is arguing against is not a policy proposed by the C.C.F. in this country or in this house, but a policy laid down years ago by Right Hon. R. B. Bennett when he was prime minister of Canada. Mr. Bennett made the point, and if I wished to prolong the debate and went up to my office I could produce numerous quotations from his speeches when the radio commission was set up, indicating that the possession of a radio wave was not an inherent right of any particular organization to which it was alienated for the time being, but must remain always under the control of the nation and it was, in fact, a monopoly of that air wave granted only temporarily. I want to tell my hon. friend that I do not believe in monopolies that may be used by private organizations to control either the industry or the thought of the country. The reason the radio commission was set up originally was that the government of the day believed, and I feel the people of Canada believe today, that we cannot safely alienate radio facilities into private hands and have freedom of thought and speech in this country.
It came to my attention a few days ago that the company developing the iron ore deposits in the Ungava district is asking the C.B.C. for the right to establish a radio station, a monopoly in that area. If they operate that radio station as they operate their railway only those who are acceptable to that company will be permitted to use that radio station. The airways are a natural monopoly which must be kept, as all monopolies must be kept, strictly under the control of this parliament, not under the control of the government but under the control of all the elected representatives of the people.
I cannot understand my hon. friend when he talks about freedom of speech and freedom of thought. What freedom of speech or thought is there over many of these radio stations? I know of organizations that have applied for time in order to answer speeches that have been made on time that has been bought by some powerful organization with the funds at its disposal. Unless you can put up an equivalent amount of money you cannot reply to the statements that were made on these radio stations. At least the C.B.C. does give to the people of Canada an opportunity of hearing all points of view without those people who hold those points of view having to buy expensive radio time in order to express their opinions. It seems to me that we have to keep very closely under the control of this parliament the radio services and facilities of this country.

My criticism of the government is that it has deserted the policies it too laid down in former years. If my memory serves me right, there was a time when it was decided that private radio stations would be limited to a certain power, I think it was 1,000 watts. Then it went to 5,000 watts; then it went to

Bit by bit we have been deserting the fundamental principle that was laid down for the radio commission, and subsequently for the broadcasting corporation when it was set up in 1936 or 1937, I forget which. I was in the house, but I have just forgotten which year. I did not expect to speak on this matter, so I did not look up the facts.
I want to see the radio corporation under the control of this parliament. I want to see freedom of speech on the air, and I want to see freedom in television. I want to see television operated in the public interest, not as an advertising agency for powerful corporations and companies that can afford to buy television time which less privileged people cannot obtain.
I do not want to see either our Canadian Broadcasting Corporation stations or the private stations dominated by United States programs. I think already this country is dominated to too great an extent by the United States. It is not that I am against the United States, or against any of the people in that country, but I want to see this country built up as Canada, as a country with its own institutions and its own way of life. I do not want to see the infiltration of United States television and radio programs to any greater extent than they have infiltrated today.
So far as the communist party is concerned, and their free time, let me say that I hold no brief for that party. Over the years it has fought me and those associated with me even more vigorously than it has fought any other political party in this country. But I want to make this perfectly clear. I believe in freedom of speech, and I do not think we shall lose anything if we stand by that principle of freedom of speech. I am not afraid of communist propaganda in this country, provided we do not allow the seed of communism to develop here and provided we do not allow poverty, misery and want to come upon this land, as it did when my hon. friends were in power in 1930, or when their successors were in power from 1935 to 1940 and nothing was done to adequately meet the situation.
The government is not following C.C.F. policy. I am convinced of this, that if it is

Supply-National Revenue C.C.F. policy then it is the policy of the Canadian people. I move around a good deal. I meet people throughout the country and in the United States who have a very high regard for the C.B.C. They realize that we would not have the development of Canadian talent on radio that we do have, were it not for the C.B.C. We would never hear plays like Julius Caesar, or other Shakespearean plays. We would not hear grand opera performed by national talent if it were not for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
The broadcasting corporation has done much to develop Canadian talent. I do not know whether hon. members on the committee had the logs of private stations before them this year for examination so they could see what some of these private radio stations are doing in connection with the development of local talent, which they are obligated to develop. But I do know when I was on that radio committee I could not find evidence of most private stations doing what they were supposed to do when they were granted a licence to operate a station and use a certain monopoly, a radio channel lent to them and to them alone, in part for the development of Canadian talent.
I want to compliment the C.B.C. upon the manner in which over these last years they have developed Canadian drama and Canadian music, both operatic and symphonic. Over the last year or so I have not listened to the radio as frequently as I used to when I was more familiar with the programs, but friends of mine tell me that over the last two years there has been a further improvement in C.B.C. programs. I cannot understand my hon. friends, who laid the foundation of our broadcasting system in this country, rising in their places and trying to destroy it, in the interests of private monopolies that would grab our newspapers-
Utter nonsense.

Well, take the Thomson
chain. How many newspapers does the Thomson chain control? How many radio stations does he control?
What has that to do with what we said?

Much. I do not want to see these private interests given control, through private radio stations and the ownership of newspapers. One of the policies we thought was laid down some years ago in a radio committee report was that newspapers should divorce themselves from radio. Yet today we have a concentration of radio and newspapers in fewer and fewer hands, and they want to do the same thing with television.

It is not the policy of the C.C.F. alone to oppose this. I am convinced it is the policy of the Canadian people, people who want freedom, and who want any monopoly carefully controlled by the government so it does not become a private monopoly to control the thought of the people.

Mr. Chairman, I have greatly enjoyed the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I do not know how one could express the ideal of managing radio any better than he has expressed it, and I congratulate him warmly. Sometimes he and I disagree, but on this occasion we are completely in accord. Our great problem is how to set up an agency whereby we can guarantee the fine principles he has laid down. That seems to be causing us more trouble than we would like to contemplate.
I have nothing but praise for the C.B.C. in respect of the matters mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I have been following the C.B.C. with considerable care during the last year, when I have had the time, and I have found that the educational, cultural and various other programs are of a high order and worthy of the highest praise, considering the handicaps and limitations under which the C.B.C. has to operate from the standpoint of geography, finance, immaturity, and all those other things which handicap the organization in its endeavours to attain its ideals.
The other matter mentioned by the hon. member, the desire on the part of the C.B.C. to give various political parties opportunities to express their views, is highly commendable. I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I do not care how many communists speak to the people, so long as the people know they are communists. It is those who sneak in and teach communism without the people knowing that they are teaching communism, or without their knowing that they are communists, who are causing the danger in this country. I do not fear having any doctrine of political or religious philosophy taught to the people or advocated before the people, so long as the other side has a similar opportunity to be heard and so long as the people know exactly who is talking, and why.
The minister and the committee will remember that last year I raised a question which I considered to be of great importance, namely the indoctrination of communism through various speakers who are heard over the C.B.C. I referred to this the other day in another connection and indicated that I proposed to have something further to say, and in greater detail, when opportunity arose.

I have had two or three people listening rather closely to the programs which have been given over the C.B.C. to the Canadian people by various speakers since I spoke a year ago or a little more, and I am basing what I am saying tonight on what they have recorded and told me. I think the ordinary individual would be surprised to hear-I may not be giving this completely, but this is what is reported to me-that we have had 19 pro-communist speakers having astonishingly free access to the programs of the C.B.C. and coming in from the United States and Britain and Canada, while we have had only four people speaking against communism and their opportunities to speak have been few and far between. That is not a very good thing to contemplate. I propose to go into some detail just to show that what I am saying is not idle.
Before I start discussing some of these speakers whose performances I have here recorded, I wish to say that those who have been keeping a record of what has been going out over the C.B.C. tell me that our own press gallery has been worthy of the very highest praise, men such as Blakely and Campbell and John Bird and Dempson and Baldwin and other members of our gallery. When they have been speaking on matters they have given the facts. They have not attempted to slant those facts. That is worthy of high praise. When I hear a capital report I want a capital report, actual and objective. I do not want too much subjective material in it. I rejoice that such a good report could be given concerning the men of our press gallery. The one submitting the comment to me says this concerning our own men:
These fellows apparently know the communist conspiracy through and through and they do not monkey around trying to feed the Canadian people the wrong thing. They stick to facts and give the Canadian people a good resume of what has taken place in parliament that week.
That, I believe, is exactly the ideal which we should have in mind no matter who performs over the C.B.C. Whether a person speaks from Britain, the United States or Canada, whether he speaks from a university or from any other place, his business should be to give facts and not his own personal opinions, especially when they happen to be contrary perhaps to what the general will of the people would have.
I am now going to mention four speakers who have spoken against communism, according to my record, and give the comment which my reporter gives me. Dr. Watson Kirk-connell is one of the great anti-communists, as everyone knows who has heard him. As far as my reporter knows, from the spring
Supply-National Revenue of 1940 to the end of 1954 Watson Kirkconnell was not once invited by the C.B.C. to speak on current events. That may not be entirely right, but that is what my informant tells me.
Then we had a man named William Rowan, of the University of Alberta, who gave a most informative talk over the C.B.C. on June 20, 1954. Why has he not had one repeat engagement? This is a part of what Rowan said:
Radio has become the voice of humanity, a mass tool of news dissemination. An informed public can only be created on the basis of factual information, not propaganda.
Another one is Jack Brayley of the Canadian Press. He gave a good talk from Korea on Syngman Rhee's popularity. I guess that is what caused him not to appear again over the C.B.C. Why is he not invited to speak once in a while instead of Robert McKenzie of the London school of economics, or Matthew Halton or Douglas LaChance?
There is another one, Leonard Schapiro, an authority on Soviet affairs, who speaks over the B.B.C., who exposed the failures of Soviet agriculture and said:
The root of the problem Is the stubborn resistance of the peasant to doctrinaire Marxist theories.
I understand he has not had a repeat performance. That is sufficient to show the kind of thing which I believe the Canadian people have a right to hear.
It developed in our discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Justice, I believe, that only 63,000 people in Canada voted communist in the 1953 election, which indicates that only 63,000 of the voting people of Canada want anything to do with communism. Yet listen to the array of speakers who are turned on them by the C.B.C. as I shall give them in a few minutes. First we have a group of liberal speakers, so-called, liberal with a small "1". The liberal speaker, as the word "liberal" is used there, usually means a pro-communist or one far to the left. There are lots of "liberals" in the United States. They are not liberal at all. Any self-respecting liberal in Canada would not be seen dead alongside one of them.
Now Bertrand Russell comes on and says, "Let us start loving the communists." That was on November 21, 1954. Well, now, that is most interesting, is it not? Ralph Lapp, a scientist from Washington, gave a strong defence for Oppenheimer the same week the United States government denounced him, on April 15, 1954. Let us stop long enough and ask was it known by the C.B.C. officials that these two men were going to speak in that way before they were put on the air? If it was not known, why was it not? In the name

What would be the idea? Who in the C.B.C. set-up chose those two men? Here is another one. The works of H. G. Wells, I am informed, were given, two or three performances after the hockey season was over last year. The hockey season was over in May, 1954. I have no particular objection to H. G. Wells, but H. It will be said, people ought to have both sides. Yes, but the trouble is people do not have the other side. That is what I objected to last year when I spoke. He said:

When Clement Attlee made his trip to red China in the fall of 1954, this newspaper wrote:
China has taken to communism dictatorship like a lost man to a signpost, a tramp to bread and cheese, a megalomaniac to Aladdin's lamp. As far as China is concerned it has found its panacea.
Now compare this with John Ridley's report in the Daily Telegraph, London, England:
I came out from communist China and it was with a feeling of immense relief. I knew China before what is now described as the liberation, and I found it was a sad, dismal place in comparison.
That is enough to give some idea of the Manchester Guardian. Now, here are some of the Manchester Guardian speeches we have had turned on us by the C.B.C. Patrick Keatley, C.B.C. "Midweek Review", July 28, 1954; a glorification of the great achievements by Chou En-lai at Geneva when Indochina was given over to the reds:
Mr, Chou had been invited by the B.B.C. to say a few words to British listeners, and he agreed. That in itself is remarkable enough.
Now, Mr. Keatley has a perfect right to say that if he wishes, but the point is that he is following the communist line. He is building up Chou En-lai and certainly giving comfort to our enemies. Francis Boyd conforms in a similar manner. Richard Scott was chosen by the C.B.C. to report the Geneva conference of the summer of 1954, direct from Geneva. Daily Mr. Scott told the Canadian people from noonday to Sunday on "Capital Report" that communism is so acceptable in Indo-China. Daily he hammered back to Canada that free elections would be won by the communists, when there have been no free elections won by the communists in any state so far as I know. His gleeful voice betrayed his red leanings and those of his paper, the choice of our C.B.C.
Now here is another Manchester Guardian speaker. Max Freedman speaks from Washington on "Capital Report" regularly, and has done so for some years. Note this man's communist line. On February 8, 1953, he said:
Millions of Americans are convinced that increased support for Chiang Kai-shek's regime on Formosa is against the enduring interests of their country.
I wish, from my personal knowledge, to add that no government in the world has a greater right than the Canadian government to protest against the implications of the new Formosa policy.
The presence of Chiang Kai-shek's troops in Korea, it was proposed, would prolong the war, would create fresh problems with communist China,
[Mr. Blackmore.l

and would leave a legacy of political troubles that would far outweigh any possible military advantages that would come from making a partner out of the discredited and discarded government on Formosa.
How could you preach a communist line in a more concentrated form, in a greater variety of respects, and for the same length of time than is done right here? And we are paying men to say these things! Right in those statements are at least three complete falsehoods. On July 19, 1953, the same man spoke. I am not going into detail concerning these, because we do not have time.
On October 4, 1953, and November 1, 1953, he spoke, and in 1954 he is still following the communist propaganda line. Freedman spoke on February 7, 1954, and in this case he would not release his script. He said that Bruce Hutchison, a very close friend of his, had "told me with regret of growing anti-American feeling in Canada". Freedman also said he hoped Chiang Kai-shek "will not resume his civil war." That is an absolute lie by implication. On February 21, 1954, he said:
It may be possible for the Republican administration to end the sullen quarantine of China that has already lasted much too long.
When has the United States government quarantined China? It has quarantined Formosa, but not China. Do you see the lie there? On June 27, 1954-and no script was released for this-Freedman intimated that: -some say in the United States that the United States state department gave China to the communists.
And-
-as if the United States state department had a title of deed to China.
-calling it a complete fraudulent charge. Another absolute lie, because the United States was the very organization that gave China to Russia. On May 1, 1955, Freedman criticized the Knowland - Bridges - Jenner-Hickenlooper policy which is against negotiations with communist China. Freedman said:
The Knowland group can be rescued from their misdemeanours by the possible errors of communist China.
No script, would be released for this one.
I ask why the Canadian people should be called upon to listen to all that kind of thing constantly.
Now I propose to give some details regarding a man against whom I spoke last year.
I have others, but I shall not have time to go all through this list. I have a large sheet of them here, including Robert McKenzie, Andre Laurendeau, Douglas LaChance, Louis C. Walmsley and Matthew Halton. Matthew Halton is listed as having spoken over our

radio system seven times, Louis C. Walmsley twice, Douglas LaChance twice, Andre Lau-rendeau six times, Robert McKenzie five times and J. B. McGeachy eight times. Here is what J. B. McGeachy said on November 14, 1954:
I've taken the view all along-since 1945-that the two halves of this divided world can live together in peace. I still think so.
There is the communist line of co-existence. We are trying to believe that it is possible to have co-existence and still keep up our guard. I hope, but we all know what Lenin said. His words have been placed on record in this house two or three times. In the light of those words no person has any right to assume that we can have peaceful co-existence. Mr. McGeachy goes on to say:
The Russians, and the Chinese as well, have a tremendous .iob to do at home in giving their people something like contentment and an economic equality with the other nations of the world . . .
There is. I think, more solid evidence that the Russians want peace.
Did the Russians act as though they wanted peace? When they came to the most recent conference they wanted to talk about Formosa and the eastern provinces. Why? To get Formosa if they could. To get red China into the UN if they could. That is what they want. They want to get us under their control completely.
On December 5, 1954, McGeachy made statements that were very strongly communist. On December 26, 1954, McGeachy set forth his policy:
At the two poles of our divided human society, Washington and Moscow, co-existence is the declared aim of foreign policy. . . . the irresistible social revolution that's going on in Asia-a revolution aimed at throwing off western domination and effecting economic changes.
That may be very correct but we wonder why in the world we should be told that over the C.B.C. What bearing has it on Canada? All it can possibly do is build up pro-communist public opinion in this democracy which can influence the United States, because we can take certain stands in the United Nations meetings and so forth. That is why there is so much concentration on Canada. On January 16, 1955, he said:
Nobody .... can defend the jailing of the airmen. This is the procedure of an outlaw, holding a captive to ransom. But let us face the fact that the United Nations (Washington in this matter has been chiefly responsible for U.N. policy) in whose service the airmen flew and fought, gives China the treatment reserved for outlaws.
I shall leave out the next portion because it does not bear particularly on what we are talking about, but here we have once more
Supply-National Revenue this slant that red China should be recognized. On February 6, 1955, we have this:
In other words, Mr. Acheson said by implication that if the communists captured Korea and Formosa, this would not disturb the United States.
We know perfectly well that Acheson said that, but we know Acheson was lying at the time he said it. McGeachy said:
It may be rash for a layman, a non-military person like myself, to venture an opinion here; but I am in good company in saying I don't believe a foothold in Formosa is necessary for the safety of the United States.
He can give that as his own private opinion, but why tell that nonsense to Canadians as a whole? There are other speeches given by this man; and I do not know of a speech I have heard by J. B. McGeachy that has not had the communist line in it somewhere. I should like to know just why these speeches go on our C.B.C. programs.
I do not wish to hold the committee up longer in order to go into these other matters, but I should like to ask this question. What is it about the C.B.C's organization, or who are pulling the strings behind the C.B.C., that causes them to be so emotionally exercised in favour of communism? That is what we want to know. By what means can that behaviour on their part be justified, when the whole Canadian people have so signally indicated their opposition to communism?
What can we do about this thing? I mentioned the matter last year but there has been no change. I cannot blame the minister. I do not blame the minister at all. He has not a chance in the world, apparently, of controlling the C.B.C. I greatly doubt that anyone in Canada or any combination of the patriotic people of Canada can control the C.B.C. as it is now being operated. I do not believe this parliament exercises a bit of control over it in matters like this. It seems to be an absolutely free agent unto itself in all matters pertaining to communism.
What must the members of this house do to bring that organization under control to the extent that it will be Canadian instead of pro-Russian? That is something 1 should like to find out. In respect of all these matters that I have indicated here it is just as pro-Russian today as though it were being directed immediately from Moscow. It could not do any better job from Moscow than is being done right now. In the light of all that kind of thing, remembering the terribly dangerous situation we are in and remembering the fact that right now it is just a question whether we can possibly survive against communism in this world, under circumstances like that I say that to have that sort

Supply-National Revenue of thing going on is simply not to be endured. As I have said, I do not blame the minister. He cannot control this outfit.

Mr. Chairman,
I am one of those who believe firmly that this session should have been a month shorter so we could go home and see our families and our electors. I therefore will not be very long, because I do not want to prolong the debate too much. However, there is one thing I do not understand after having listened to the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Lethbridge, and it is this. How is it that the C.B.C. should support lecturers advocating communist ideals on the one hand, and on the other hand be trying, on the shortwave, to go behind the iron curtain and impress upon the people behind the iron curtain that our way of living is better than communism? I do not understand how they could support those speaking on the air in Canada in favour of communism, and at the same time tell the people behind the iron curtain that our way of living or our political philosophy is better than theirs.
That is what I cannot understand.

I do not understand that. I do not think the C.B.C. is putting up a double front. If I thought there were some body or some organization behind the C.B.C. in favour of developing communist ideas or philosophy in our population, I would not be the last to ask in this chamber for a clean-up of the whole organization.
I am sure that is right.

I now wish to say just a word about a few ideas expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, when he said that Mr. Dunton had advocated the present set-up of the C.B.C. organization in co-operation and sometimes in competition with the privately-owned stations. In 1928 the Aird commission arrived at this conclusion. The interests of the listening public and of the nation could be served adequately only-
-by some form of public ownership, operation and control behind which is the national power and prestige of the whole public of Canada.
That is the conclusion of the Aird report. In 1932, while Mr. Bennett was at the head of the government, a special parliamentary committee came to general conclusions similar to those of the Aird commission and made recommendations with regard to the setting up of a public radio body. It was the C.R.B.C. The committee in 1934-always at the same time Mr. Bennett was prime minister of Canada-maintained the same principles of public ownership and control.
I wanted to put that on the record in order to emphasize the ideas expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I wish to add something I have always believed, namely that the C.B.C. and its organization, starting with the chairman and the other officials, have always lived up to their responsibilities. I think the words used by Mr. Dunton in the committee on June 4, 1946, were right and were coming from a sincere man. He said this:
We have a keen sense of our responsibility to the public through parliament and we feel it is of great value to the corporation and an important guarantee to the public that its affairs and policies be studied by a committee such as this one.
I have been on that committee since 1945. Every time the C.B.C. has been called before the committee to answer questions of the members, they have done so in the best spirit that could be wished for. I congratulate the officials of the C.B.C. for the way they have handled this organization from the very beginning. I am one of those who favour the-present set-up.
Even if I do not agree with the opinions of others in this house, I am going to say that I am against a special regulatory body. But before dealing with this matter I am. going to quote from the Massey report. In quoting from the Massey report and expressing the ideas contained in that report, I am going to express my own ideas because I have made those ideas mine. At page 276 of the Massey report, chapter 18, we find this:
First, radio may be regarded primarily as a. means of entertainment, a by-product of tha advertising business. Such a view does not imply

that it may not be used for education, for enlightenment and for the cultivation of taste; all these bring entertainment to many people. On the other hand, radio, as one of the most powerful means of education, may be regarded as a social influence too potent and too perilous to be ignored by the state which, in modern times, increasingly has assumed responsibility for the welfare of its citizens. This second view of radio operation assumes that this medium of communication is a public trust to be used for the benefit of society, in the education and the enlightenment as well as for the entertainment of its members.
Those are my ideas on broadcasting. I think most of the members-I could say all the members in this chamber-admit that we have a bilingual country and that we are bicultural. We want to keep those great advantages. According to what I have just read from the Massey report, I am afraid if we have a separate regulatory body this situation of bilingualism will suffer. I know I do not speak for everyone, but that is my belief.
If you look at the minority report of the Massey commission you will see what the privately-owned radio stations think. It is normal to have this in mind because it is their own money they have risked. They want to have a return on their money. Mr. Surveyer, at page 387. says this:
No private station could carry on a program policy such as that of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or such as requested by some of the associations without running into financial difficulties.
This means that the privately-owned stations cannot do the same job the C.B.C. is doing in Canada, or in any district where there is a minority of French-speaking Canadians who would like to have French programs. If these private stations go into the red, as Mr. Allard said in answer to a question put to him by the hon. member for Saskatoon, in trying to maintain French programs, they are not there to lose money and they will stop. It is normal. These French-speaking minorities in Canada would suffer if we did not have the C.B.C. operating in the way it has been operating in the past. I am afraid that a separate regulatory body would not be able to keep up its responsibilities toward the French-speaking minority outside of Quebec. It is for that reason that I am against a separate regulatory body and in favour of the C.B.C.
I want to thank the hon. member for Eglinton for the very kind words he expressed about me as chairman of this committee. I must tell him that the sentiments he expressed tonight should have been directed to every member of this committee. My duties were very easy to perform because of the perfect co-operation I received from every member of the special committee on broad-
Supply-National Revenue casting. I wish publicly, in this house, to thank all those members for their friendly co-operation.
It was said that free time should not have been given to the communist party during federal elections. If I understood correctly, it was also stated that the communist party had no free time on the B.B.C. in the last general election in England. Did I hear the hon. member for Eglinton correctly?
That was the evidence given to the committee.

I have gone to the trouble of getting some information on that point. If the communists want to have free time on the B.B.C. they have to have 50 candidates running. The membership in the British House of Commons is over 600. In Canada the communists are obliged to run 66 candidates, and our membership is only 265. If we want to compare the two situations I would say the Canadian attitude is much better than the British attitude. It is more rigid than the British attitude, 50 candidates when the membership in the house is 600, as compared to 66 candidates when the membership in the Canadian house is 265. Our policy is more rigid.
But the fact is they did not get any free time on the B.B.C.
Because they did not put up 50 candidates.
They had 30 candidates.

In England the communists have to put up 50 candidates when the membership in the house is 600, and the membership in the Canadian house is 265 but we oblige them to put up 66 candidates. Our policy is more rigid toward the communists having free time than it is in England.
I said I did not want to delay the committee any more because I am anxious to go back home to my family and electors. It is my pleasure to thank the members of the committee for their very great and friendly cooperation.

The subject with which I am going to deal for a few moments is a rather dry one. I shall try to make it as brief and concise as possible. I intend to deal with two clauses in the final report of the broadcasting committee dated June 17. The first clause appears at page 815 of the committee's proceedings, and reads:
Your committee examined at length the financial statements of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and considered its accounting methods. The committee is of the opinion that such accounting methods have been improved since the Auditor General's report of August 5. 1954. and recommends

Supply-National Revenue that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should continue its studies to modernize and further improve all its accounting practices.
I should like to refer to the bottom of page 809 of these proceedings, to simply point out that the item of the minutes in connection with paragraph 12 reads:

, seconded by Mr. Richardson,
That paragraph 12 be amended by deleting the last sentence thereof and substituting the following:
The committee is of the opinion that such accounting methods have been improved since the Auditor General's report of August 5, 1954, and recommends that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should continue its studies to modernize and further improve all its accounting practices.
After discussion, and the question having been put, the said motion was resolved in the affirmative.
The reason I have mentioned that, Mr. Chairman, is simply that I would like to point out that the motion was seconded by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, and that the amendment was agreed to by a Liberal majority of that committee. Let me refer to the actual meat of this amendment:
.	. . that such accounting methods have been
improved since the Auditor General's report of August 5, 1954, and recommends that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should continue its studies to modernize and further improve all its accounting practices.
To me that can only mean one thing. There has been some improvement since August 5, 1954. That is the report of the committee. Also it recommends that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should continue its studies to modernize and to further improve. In other words the committee agreed that the present system of accounting, and accounting methods, did need modernization and bringing up to date.
Mr. Chairman, I propose to set before the house what in my opinion is rather definite evidence bearing out the contention that the accounting methods of the C.B.C. certainly have needed improvement in the past, and continue to need that improvement. In this connection I should like to read a couple of paragraphs from the Auditor General's report for the year 1951-52. This appears at page 53, volume II of the public accounts for that year, and is as follows:
It is some years since the [DOT] information in the detailed records was confirmed by reference to the assets at each location. However a stocktaking is now in progress. Until this has been completed and necessary accounting adjustments made it remains impracticable to verify by audit whether the shown values correctly represent existing assets.
The next item is "Allowance for depreciation and obsolescence" and it states:
Sound broadcasting; fixed assets, $3,201,690.
It is recommended that when stocktaking is completed appropriate action be taken with respect to rates of depreciation and obsolescence. Those used by the corporation through the years have

never been scientifically determined nor consistently applied with the consequence that the appropriateness of the $3,201,690 allowance is open to question.
Mr. Chairman, the 1952-53 Auditor General's report appears at page 51 of the corporation's annual report for that year. I should like to read two or three paragraphs from this particular report. It refers first to fixed assets of $10,656,455. I might interject that this is of course, you will understand, one year later. It says:
In recent years audit verification of moveable assets was impracticable, as no stocktakings had been done. However it was noted in the 1951-52 report that one was then in progress. This was completed during the 1952-53 fiscal year, and it was found that there were items on the books to a value of $91,931, which were not reflected in the stocktaking. An investigation of the discrepancy commenced by the corporation had not been completed at the close of the audit.
The next item is, "Allowance for depreciation and obsolescence."
In the 1951-52 report it was suggested that when stocktaking was completed action be taken with respect to rates of depreciation and obsolescence since the appropriateness of the accumulated allowance was open to question for the reason that the rates used through the years had never been scientifically established or consistently applied. The comment still applies.
And then the heading, "Books of account".
The accounts are kept on a cash basis, except at the year end when accruals are entered in order that the annual financial statement may be prepared. The reason given by the corporation's officers for not maintaining the books on an accrual basis, as is generally the practice in corporate accounting, is that the cash basis better serves the corporation's internal administrative requirements.
Now I would like to read from the report of August 5, 1954, at page 51. This is one year later than the report I just read. The heading is, "Allowance for depreciation and obsolescence" and states:
Still applicable is the comment in previous reports to the effect that the appropriateness of the accumulated allowance for depreciation and obsolescence is open to question, for the reason that the rates used through the years have never been scientifically established or consistently applied.
And the next item:
Weaknesses having been noted in the accounts, this office wrote to the chairman of the board of governors on October 23, 1952 with supporting details and concluding with the words-
And these are the concluding words:
It is suggested that the system be carefully reviewed and appropriately revised and co-ordinated so that there may be no need to qualify the audit certificate in this regard.
That is the end of the quotation from the letter. Then, going on with the report: Subsequent action by the corporation not having been of a nature to remedy the situation, the

manner in which the accounts were kept during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954 was not found to be conducive to satisfactory audit.
This last report refers to a letter dated October 23, 1952, and I am afraid I must read all of it. It is addressed to Mr. A. D. Dunton, chairman of the board of governors, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and says:
Part VIII of the Financial Administration Act having been proclaimed effective as from October 1, 1952, the auditors of crown corporations now are required, by section 87, to report more extensively than before. Among other things, they are to report whether proper books of account have been kept. I now write as you may wonder what is the position in so far as the C.B.C. is concerned.
At present the accounts do not conform with accepted corporate accounting practice. They are on a cash, rather than an accrual basis. In consequence, they do not show month by month the financial state of the assets and liabilities, neither do they correctly disclose what are the to-date revenues and expenditures for the year. Furthermore, information provided monthly for the guidance of management, which normally would and according to accepted accounting practice should be available from the books of account, is assembled in memorandum records not controlled by the books subjected to audit by this office.
An interim test audit for the five months ended August 31, 1952 revealed several unsatisfactory features as exemplified by the following:
(1)	It is the practice at the close of each fiscal year to credit accounts payable with the invoices then unpaid and to charge the relative expense and asset accounts. In effect, this places the accounts on an accrual basis at the year end. Therefore, to return them to a cash basis, it is necessary at the beginning of a new year to make a reversal of this entry. At the tune of the audit such a reversal had not been made. As a result, the balance shown as owing for accounts payable included accounts paid several months ago.
(2)	Claims made over several months for reimbursement of expenditures for the international shortwave service were not entered: consequently, the repayment received from the government appeared as a liability of $272,050.
(3)	Although more than $4,800,000 had been received, no revenue from licence fees was reflected in the accounts; instead the amount was incorrectly shown as a liability to the Department of Transport.
In view of the foregoing and because the accounts do not provide adequate internal control, it is suggested that the system be carefully reviewed, and appropriately revised and co-ordinated so that there may be no need to qualify the audit certificate in this regard.
This letter was dated October 23, 1952, and was signed by J. Hopkinson, assistant auditor general. It is to be found on page 396 of the proceedings of the committee. I think it is right to mention that in one of these criticisms, the July 10, 1953, report, mention was made of a discrepancy of $91,931 between the book account and the actual stocktaking. Evidence presented to the committee was to the effect that this had been considerably reduced, but undoubtedly there would still have to be some write-off.
Supply-National Revenue
I think you will have to agree, Mr. Chairman, that in this sequence of events, first the letter, the Auditor General's report concerning the 1951-52 accounts of the corporation, the Auditor General's reports in 1952-53 and in 1953-54, and the letter dated October 23, 1952, to Mr. Dunton, there must have been some laxity some place along the line. The first mention of this discrepancy in accounting goes back to 1951-52. The letter to Mr. Dunton mentions that only as of October 1, 1952, does the Auditor General of necessity report on the system of accounts. How are we to know? I think we have every reason to suspect that this system of accounting has gone back over the years. The Auditor General has found every fault with it. I think that speaks for itself.
Following the Auditor General's report of March 5, 1954, the firm of P. S. Ross and Sons, chartered accountants, was engaged to examine the accounting system. On February 7, 1955, they presented a report. This report is of a preliminary nature, and at the moment I certainly am not prepared to say that it is the cure-all or that any cure has been found. In fact, on page 399 of the proceedings Mr. Dunton had this to say:
It is not a question of an interim or final report. They were asked basic questions concerning cash, accrual and commitments and so on, and I think it is right to say that they gave their answers to the questions. However, a number of questions arise from carrying that out, and our management would want further opinions from them as to the practicality and the cost and the method of carrying out some of their recommendations. There was also a recommendation concerning the difference in the opinions expressed in brief form by the Auditor General and what chartered accounts say.
The words "chartered accounts" appear here. I presume that is a typographical error and it should be "what chartered accountants say". Further down the witness says:
I perhaps did not make it clear that this is not an interim report. This is simply a report in which they answer questions asked by us. We are going to ask for further information, advice and study from them, arising out of certain suggestions they have made in their first report.
I think it can be said that some consideration has been given and is still being given to this report of P. S. Ross and Sons. In my estimation there is a long, long way to go. The committee of this house has recommended in paragraph 12:
That the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should continue its studies to modernize and further improve all its accounting practices.
This unsatisfactory condition, Mr. Chairman, has existed at least, as I mentioned before, since the 1951-52 accounting period, and undoubtedly beforehand. To my way of thinking some action should have been taken

Supply-National Revenue as far back as the date of the letter from the Auditor General to Mr. Dunton dated October 23, 1952. The first action that was taken followed the August 5, 1954, report, two full years afterward. All I can say is, what would a meeting of shareholders think of management if they had received a report from the auditors of their company two years before any action was taken to rectify the situation?
I simply state it is apparent that the committee is not satisfied with the progress in improving those methods and in modernizing the accounting.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to paragraph 17, to be found on page 816 of the committee's proceedings. It is paragraph 17 of the final report, which reads as follows: Your committee feels that the present system of financing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in the light of increasing operating costs, should be reviewed to ensure a continual expansion of the national television service. In this connection the committee agrees that it is essential for the corporation to continue to supplement the income it receives from public sources with revenues from commercial operations.
I would point out, of course, that that paragraph is in the report, yes; but at the bottom of page 810 of the committee's proceedings there is the following:
On paragraph 17:

Mr. Chairman, I move
That the committee rise, report progress and leave to sit again.
Motion negatived: Yeas, 29; nays, 35.

Mr. Chairman, on behalf members of this party I want to endorse sentiments expressed by the hon. mem for Eglinton with respect to the court shown the committee by the chairman of C.B.C. and his officials who were called give evidence. I rise at this time to sup] a principle which I believe is the only that can give the Canadian people the t; of broadcast program, both sound and t vision, they deserve. If pressure should brought by public opinion to change the p cies now followed by the C.B.C. we may in danger of losing that body. Therefoi feel obliged to bring before the Canac

people why I believe the C.B.C. is the only body in a position to give the type of service which is so necessary.
I feel that there have been no new arguments interjected into this debate to describe the operations of the C.B.C., and therefore anything I might say would only be repetition. Until new arguments are brought forward I feel that we in this group are justified in supporting the principle of the C.B.C.
It is all too easy for people not in the know as to the problems which must be faced under what is termed a single service, all the technical difficulties not only in respect to population but geographic, to offer unfair criticism. I think most of the criticism is based on lack of knowledge, and if the necessary information were available much of this criticism would not be forthcoming. It is my opinion that we want to still have the present control that is being exercised-I believe that is very important in the light of the tremendous expansion in this country-over this greatest medium of this day and age for good and evil. Television has the greatest possible influence over the Canadian people, especially young people. Because of the danger that is inherent in television broadcasting, it is absolutely essential to have some control that has the interest of the Canadian people at heart.
If there were any doubt in my mind as to the ability of the committee members to obtain information from the witnesses, that doubt was removed when I sat on the committee. The questions that were asked brought very frank answers that gave in great detail the operations of the C.B.C. They left no doubt in anybody's mind that it was a fair way of carrying on an investigation.
