I fail to see that any regulatory body such as is suggested by the Conservative party would justify its existence in any way, provided that it did not have, as they suggested, any ulterior motive. They suggest that such a body would not have any ulterior motives.
From my observations in the committee it would not justify its existence. After all, the people of Canada are going to continue to be asked to subsidize broadcasting in this country. Therefore the only people who have a right to carry on the investigation of such a body as the C.B.C. are the elected representatives of the people. I do not know where you would find a group of people fairer than those who represent the people in that committee.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, it is a matter of record that the C.B.C. regulations, as they are presently being carried out, are and have been subscribed to by the Conservative party.
Supply-National Revenue They were brought into this house as a resolution by the Conservative party. I often wonder where these champions of so-called democracy who speak about free competition were prior to the establishment of the C.B.C. It is something we have become accustomed to. When an industry starts out in its infancy and there is a great risk involved, we find that in many cases private interests are very reluctant to risk their capital in such a venture. Once it has been proven to be successful, as in the case of the C.B.C., then we find a great agitation on the part of private interests to get into what has proven to be a fairly lucrative field.
They talk about competition. I cannot see very much competition when the Canadian people are asked to put up in the neighbourhood of $100,000 a year toward the maintenance of every private broadcasting station that is licensed in this country. It is no wonder that the private broadcasters in this country are in a lucrative field, for the simple reason that they are being provided with a large portion of their broadcasts at the expense of the Canadian people. They are certainly not showing by their actions that they are prepared to give a better type of program, a better type of television show than is being shown at the present time. If they had any intention in that regard they would make it known at this time.
I suggest that if television or sound programs are to be developed in this country, talent will have to be developed. I do not think the private broadcasting people in this country have gone out of their way to develop talent to the satisfaction of anyone. I should like to read from a news item in connection with this question. I have already put it on the record, but I should like to put it on the record again:
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation gives generous assistance to Canadian composers through public performance of Canadian works over its stations, while less assistance is given by private radio stations, the Canadian league of composers said in a brief last week to the royal commission on copyright.
If the private radio stations are going to contribute, as they say they will, to a better type of program than the C.B.C., they should show more evidence of that than they are showing at the present time. I should like to comment for a moment on the brief published by the Canadian association of radio and television broadcasters and presented to the committee on broadcasting which met during this session. After reading this brief I think possibly they have made the weakest case of all. I should like to quote one or two

Supply-National Revenue items which I find in this to substantiate my contention that the case is very weak. First of all they say:
Competitive television will provide better and more effective service. It will tend to reduce, as experience in radio broadcasting has shown, the unduly large number of Canadians now regularly viewing United States television stations, in areas where only one Canadian signal is available. In the areas concerned few viewers have a second or alternative service in Canada they can turn to, so they must obtain that alternative service from American stations.
I have heard a good deal of criticism in that regard, but to anyone who has viewed the United States programs it is an entirely different picture to what you see in Canada. We must not fail to realize that at considerable cost the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is procuring the best programs that are being made in the United States. I do not think anybody would be very much impressed with the type of show that is put over the air in the United States.
I cannot easily understand committee members bringing up the point that possibly some of the channels we are not using will be used by United States broadcasters. There could be nothing more fallacious than that argument. Yet we find a responsible body like the one from which I am quoting, namely the Canadian association of radio and television broadcasters, trying to make that one of their key arguments in connection with this problem of competition. I should like to read what they have to say in that regard:
If channels available in these areas for use are not employed by Canada, there is serious danger that these or adjacent channels will be employed by the United States.
They thus leave the impression that these channels are something like any product you might buy in the store; that you can pick up, put it under your arm and walk off with it. That is just absolute nonsense. The only way in which the Americans can possibly get any of these channels that we are alleged not to be using would be to annex some of the land that now belongs to Canada. You just cannot do that with any television channel. I therefore feel that that is one of the poorest arguments that could possibly be made.
In connection with the argument as to the quality of programs now being offered by the C.B.C., and the contention that under private ownership, because of competition, the Canadian people would be exposed to better programs, I should like to quote from the report of the Massey commission:
The private owners of broadcasting as "an industry", and their stations "hardly rate a pass on cultural programs". Too many stations "regulated in principle by the C.B.C., offer programs which must be described as regrettable". In a

sampling of five stations, there was "no attempt to fulfil the proper function of the local stations... to reflect the life and interests of the community, and to use and develop local talent available ... Spot announcements crowd their programs . . . Only very rarely can limited revenue be advanced as an extenuating circumstance for this inexpensive and unimaginative programming".
Therefore do not think we need be alarmed as to the type of program that would be forthcoming because of the transfer from the C.B.C. to private stations.
There is one question I should like to have answered by the department, and it is one that I feel was not answered at all in the committee. It is a question that was raised by the hon. member for Eglinton, and it has to do with the station in Newfoundland. In the face of the fact that the C.B.C. board of governors recommended that they establish a station at St. John's in Newfoundland, I should like to know why that application was turned down and a licence was granted to a private station, namely the Newfoundland Broadcasting Company. I should like to know why the government turned down the application of the C.B.C. in spite of the fact that the C.B.C. requested that they establish a station in Newfoundland.
In conclusion I should just like to say this. I think the whole problem we have to face as responsible members in this House of Commons is this. What kind of television and what kind of sound broadcasting are we going to have in this country? I do not think anything short of what we have now is going to do the job. I believe that those difficulties which I pointed out, both geographically and because of our sparse population, dictate- and I say this without any hesitation-that the government of Canada is going to have to subsidize broadcasting in this country. I think it is absolutely justified that we should do that.
I should like to add something to what the hon. member for Portneuf said in respect of minority groups in this country. I think we in this country have become great because of our people's tolerance and our attitude towards the many minority groups in this country. We could have had a great deal of strife in this country, but because of our tolerance toward these people we have been able to arrive at a great deal of unity. I think C.B.C. television in particular can take a great deal of credit for being able to make that unity a reality. I therefore believe that what we have to do in this country is subsidize broadcasting. I feel that it is justified. I am in support of the policies and principles at present being followed. I hope nothing will happen that will cause us to lose that kind of system.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

Mr. Chairman, as one whose privilege it was to serve with others on the committee appointed to study the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the revenue, expenditures and over-all development of that corporation -and I would say that expressive corporation -I wish to present to the committee certain observations and personal conclusions.
I was one of the new members of that committee, and I look back with a great deal of pleasure at having had the opportunity to be associated with the very fine spirit which prevailed among all the members of that committee. There were 26 members, a majority of whom were from the Liberal ranks. There were only five Conservatives, two C.C.F. members and two Social Credit members.
I think it is proper for me to say that we were fortunate indeed in having had as our chairman the hon. member for Portneuf. He guided the meetings very ably and showed the kind of spirit which I consider to be a highly essential characteristic of a good chairman, especially when there are such a large number of members from the government side. I refer to a sympathetic understanding of the position of the minority members whose views in many respects were opposed to those of the government supporters.
I am sure that by this time all the members in the committee have read the final and official report of that committee. I have read it several times. As a matter of fact, tonight I have read it two or three times. It contains a truthful description of what was done; but as I read it, it seems to me that it has a general tone of approval of all things. In my humble estimation it does not reflect enough of the undercurrent of dissent which was prevalent through most of the hearings, even on the part of one of the Liberal members.
I realize that it is not the practice of this house to permit a minority report but perhaps there may be merit in considering, for the future, attaching to such final and official report of a committee a minority review. The reason for this suggestion is that time is of the greatest essence in this house. Such a report would eliminate the need of repeating dissenting arguments. It would provide the basis for members to gain the facts and figures which they need in order to take an active part at this point in our proceedings when we are considering the estimates of the department.
First of all let us take into consideration the job the committee had. Broadcasting by television and by radio is a gigantic business
Supply-National Revenue in Canada, and each has similar problems. Only by remembering this fact can we understand that while the committee sat for some 35 hearings, even that length of time, it appeared at least to me, was insufficient for every single member to examine all the intricate details of revenues, expenditures and over-all cost unless, of course, one encroached upon the time of his colleagues. Further, it would have required the full time of a member and also ample assistance in research.
Now, please do not misunderstand me. I am not saying the committee did not do a good job. It will continue to do a good job, as is always the case when the public's representatives have an opportunity of questioning and examining the administrators of the public's affairs. What I am saying, however, is that the magnitude of the job we had to perform was such that, in my opinion, we scratched only the surface of perhaps the most important question, namely the growing role which governments play in the life of this nation. We did not provide a satisfactory answer to just how far or to what extent we could allow the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to retain its special powers. For these reasons, and because it is in the public interest whose money assists the activities of this corporation, I believe we should have the strictest parliamentary review made each year of this and any other crown corporation whose call upon the public treasury is becoming costlier to the taxpayer year by year.
It must be remembered that last year there was no such committee studying the operations of the C.B.C. The last time this committee sat was in 1953. Therefore, for reasons which are psychological, namely keeping people on their toes, I do suggest that a committee of parliament be appointed, not each alternate session but each session, to study at least some of the important branches of the activities of this corporation and thereby ensure that the people of Canada keep tab on the expenditures. I say this because it seems to me that the function of the committee, under growing government control and the numerous crown corporations, is to be alert to all the hazards and implications of this growth in government. There is a lot of truth in the saying that often democracy buries itself under the load it insists on carrying.
I am not here to shed compliments on the C.B.C. My responsibility is to criticize them, but in doing that I want to be fair. I will say this, that the C.B.C. and its officials have had to stand up to some pretty scorching public comment. How many other crown corporations have to appear on the witness

Supply-National Revenue stand and give an accounting? What are the essential facts we must have in order to know what policy we should adopt with respect to the future activities of this corporation? I think anyone who is fair will be impressed by the remarkable growth and accomplishments of the corporation. It is in this very growth and in these accomplishments that we have the problems which face us. Several years ago radio and television were novelties in the experimental stage. Today they are features of everyday living.
Our people today look to the activities of the corporation as a reliable source of information, entertainment and education. What does this imply? It implies that there is a need for a still fuller nation-wide service. I maintain that if we are to have that fuller service, then we should also have the private broadcasting stations and interests to share the burdens with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I do not think anybody in this business of radio and television broadcasting in Canada should have special powers to regulate the activities of his competitor. This growth I have just mentioned also means that we should guard those things which are essential to our way of life. This can best be done by giving impartial treatment to all the news commentaries which the people have to hear.
I mention the impartial treatment of news because considerable debate took place on that very subject. It was charged that the C.B.C. had used a handful of commentators on its better conference and news programs, and that sometimes these commentators were not free of political bias or, in any event, their technique was slanted. Whether or not that was true I am not going to say. But I will say that I have had representations made to me by people in my own constituency who have been offended. This is nothing new. It has been going on for some time. I have a little article here appearing in the Financial Times of January 29, 1954, which makes reference to this charge. The headline reads: "C.B.C. Whiplash for Government". The article refers to something that was written by Chester Bloom, and it reads as follows:
The gist of what this dogged deadline devotee has to say is that if you don't like the Liberal government, the C.B.C. won't give you time on the radio. Of course it is true.
I do not so much blame the C.B.C. officials as I do the Liberal government.
He goes on to say that if someone hiccups in a way that could be construed as sounding Tory, then he is immediately banned. I continue to read:
To keep out of trouble, the C.B.C. minions simply keep the offending person off the air.
It is notorious that not a few scribes fawn on the government, and get steady assignments. Those who don't get-the air!
One would-be radio speaker has looked in vain for 14 years for an assignment because of this jittery ban. Yet another fellow can hardly get his clothes unpacked upon arrival in the city before he is breathlessly rushed to the radio.
A writer who is known not to favour the government, or whose free punching the craven C.B.C. fears, is told that he lisps, or he speaks too fast, or his voice does not reproduce too well. This is all apple sauce.
Or he may be told:	"Like to oblige you, old
man, but you know all our booking is done in Toronto. Why don't you write so and so?"
Now this is obviously a lie, because the endless flock of willing syllable stooges here in Ottawa are given radio assignments all the time.
The Liberal government will not, and cannot stand criticism. You say one bad word about the St. Laurent regime and you are through. The C B C crowd just do not want to risk their own liiy-white necks, lest Doc McCann or some other cabinet minister object.
Any criticism which does not suit the^ government is regarded as "unfair". Anything that nleases the government is called "impartial .
I think we should make it perfectly clear that the purpose of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is to give public service, not political service or patronage. I have confidence that the officers of the corporation will study this entire question and, if necessary, treat ruthlessly anyone who might use a nonpolitical program in a politically biased manner.
How about this question of television? Several years ago television appeared, but very few homes had it. It was looked upon as a luxury item. I believe regular television broadcasting did not start until the year 1952 in Montreal and Toronto. It is interesting to note that since that time, as of April 1, over 1,241,000 television sets exist in homes in Canada. I think it should now be our policy to try to bring within the range of the poor and the lowest wage earner in our country the means to acquire this instrument in order that they may enjoy some of the benefits. The C.B.C. talks of expanding their service, but one way to expand the service is to extend relief from the high costs of these instruments. We should be thinking in terms of gradual liquidation of the 15 per cent excise tax which is at the moment applied to radio and television receivers and associated products. I think this tax is a classic example of the public having to pay twice for the same service. In addition to substantial grants which the C.B.C. receives from the public treasury, it also receives revenue from the 15 per cent excise tax.
I have in my hand a letter from the radiotelevision manufacturers' association of Canada, dated May 18, 1955, which was sent to

tie Minister of Finance. I think it contains ome rather interesting information for the ommittee. It says:
Our members feel that it may not be generally ealized that the amount of excise tax collected n television receivers and tubes alone in the seal year ended March 31. 1955 was approximately 22 million, and that this amount was more than ouble the maximum that it was estimated would e collected for the C.B.C. by this method in any ne year when the plan was introduced two years go.
And later on:
Our members also feel that it may not be lenerally realized that since the 15 per cent excise ax is just as much an element of cost in a tele-rision receiver as the cabinet, the loudspeaker or my component, the distributor and dealer and inance company, if time payments are involved, nust deal with this added cost, and by the time he receivers are in Canadian homes the $22 mil-ion for the C.B.C. has actually meant close to 140 million out of the pockets of the consuming rnblic.
In statements before the committee Mr. Dunton estimated that in 1955-56 the corporation spending would be about $42,200,000. Government grants and revenues were expected to total $32,845,000. This would imply a deficit of $10,805,000 after receiving federal grants of some $25,800,000.
The reasons I mention those figures are twofold. First, while much of that cost may be necessary, that very fact indicates the need of frugality in the activities of the corporation. Second, despite the various revenues which the corporation has at this time, it appears to be facing a financial crisis. I think the C.B.C. is as anxious as anybody else to put their dealings on a sound business basis. Perhaps it is time, as was suggested this evening, to ensure to them a substantial definite grant voted by parliament each year to enable them to carry on the good work they are doing. There may be disadvantages to that proposal, but I think it has marked advantages as well. First, it would enable simpler bookkeeping and easier examination of their fiscal policy. It would ensure proper budgeting and planning and, what is very important as far as the taxpayers of this country are concerned, it will force them to make ends meet.
One of the most controversial points brought up during the committee hearings was on the question of C.B.C. policy in the matter of television, namely the so-called single-channel policy. As I understand it, under this policy only single stations are allowed to operate in any area of the country. These areas are now served by government-owned stations or by privately-owned stations. In those areas served by privately-owned stations the government has agreed not to enter into competition. In those areas
Supply-National Revenue served by government-owned stations, private initiative is denied the right to compete and give service.
The paradox of all this lies in the fact that this so-called single channel policy has created a government monopoly in those areas in which the C.B.C. operates; and on the other hand the policy sustains, although to a lesser degree, exclusive possession of service in the areas served by privately-owned stations for only those already there. I say to a lesser degree, so far as the latter is concerned, because at the present time the C.B.C. does have its stations in the larger urban centres of Canada.
Briefly, I think such a policy is diametrically opposed to the principle of a free society. One of the speakers this evening spoke of monopoly. So far as I am concerned monopoly is dangerous. It is contrary to the principle of equal opportunity, and smacks too much of "take it or leave it". It certainly denies the right to people in our country to an alternative choice.
Before going on I wish to make it amply clear that I am not arguing against the C.B.C., nor am I particularly interested in the private broadcasting stations. I do believe that some of the regulatory powers of the C.B.C. have created a great deal of bad feeling and have lent themselves to improper interpretation so far as the people of Canada are concerned.
Many years ago the great statesman in the country to the south of us, Abraham Lincoln, stated that the legitimate object of government is to do for the people what needs to be done but which they cannot, by individual effort, do at all or do so well for themselves.
I believe those people who were responsible for the founding of the C.B.C. in the early days must have had that idea in mind. It is granted that at that time special powers and controls were necessary for the corporation, if it was to provide a national service and unite the Canadian people. But today the facts indicate that over 80 per cent of our population is in a position to hear and see most of the broadcasting services. Yet that control seems to be vested permanently in the C.B.C.
I do not think any private broadcasting company, or any sensible and fair-minded member, will deny that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has made a marvellous contribution to this country. However, in the words of the submission made by the Canadian association of radio and television broadcasters, this appears:
Yet virtually all legislation pertaining to wireless communications is based upon broadcasting s development and position more than a quarter

Supply-National Revenue century ago-when this form of mass communication was in its infancy, when broadcasting's development and its present place in the community could not have been foreseen.
I do believe that public interest would be best served by giving opportunities to those so interested to make investments in this connection. I think such investments would spell out employment and higher standards. These would come by reason of competition, and it would give greater utilization to Canadian talent. But this cannot be, if the C.B.C. retains unaltered its single-channel policy. Surely the very able minister in charge of this department must have had this in mind when he stated on March 30, 1953, in the House of Commons, the following:
The principle of one station to an area is to apply only until an adequate national television system is developed. At the rate that applications for stations are now being received it may not be long before there is a sufficient degree of national coverage to justify the government and the C.B.C. giving consideration to permitting two and perhaps in some cases more than two stations in certain areas. It is anticipated that, in due course, private stations will be permitted in areas covered by C.B.C. stations, and the C.B.C. may establish stations in some areas originally covered by private stations.
It is quite apparent that what I am arguing for is the establishment of an independent regulatory board for Canadian broadcasting which, in the words of the submission made by the Canadian association of radio and television broadcasters, dated May 24, 1955, reads as follows:
1.	There be now permitted licensing of non-government television broadcasting stations in all areas of Canada, including Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, Winnipeg, Ottawa, and Halifax. This would now be consistent with the recommendations of the Massey commission, with the general outline of previous government policy statements, and would give Canadians in these areas a choice of more than one television program at one time from Canadian sources.
2.	There be created an independent regulatory board for Canadian broadcasting, to correct the present situation in which one body competes and regulates at the same time; to bring broadcasting regulation into harmony with parallel regulatory situations in all parts of Canada; and with like situations in every part of the democratic world, and so to create for Canadian broadcasting a regulatory structure based upon fundamental democratic principles.
That brings me, sir, to perhaps the most compelling reason why there should be a separate, impartial board co-ordinating the activities of the C.B.C. and the private broadcasting stations in this country. I think everybody will agree that radio and television provide one of the most effective means of influencing and moulding public opinion. Repeated often enough and with visual aid, the spoken word can be both a builder and a destroyer. In "Mein Kampf" Adolf Hitler

makes repeated reference to the power of the spoken word. I believe, therefore, that a Canadian agency in charge of the affairs of both the C.B.C. and private broadcasting is desirable, since such an agency will be divorced from government domination and from private pressure groups.
I realize that we all have confidence in Mr. Dunton and his excellent officers. I am sure the government members will have confidence in their government. While it may be that we do not fear there would be a misuse of power, let us also remember that neither this government nor anyone else is wiser than some of the lessons of past history.
In conclusion I should like to say a few words on one of the important branches of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, namely the international service. This is an agency which does not take its policy directives from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation but performs to the tune which is brought in from the Department of External Affairs. Mr. Dunton admitted that the Department of External Affairs guided the policy of the international service. From the very beginning, Mr. Chairman, I do believe the people of Canada have supported the international service; for they were led to believe that this service was an essential one, representing a very valuable psychological weapon to the free world. I believe our people insist that it continue to perform that initial function for which it was designed. I believe there have been restrictive policies on the part of external affairs, or whoever is responsible for that particular policy, as it is reflected in the international service, so that today the international service is only an anaemic semblance of what it originally was intended to be.
If you study the policy declarations that have been made throughout the years you can see that restraining influence in the very wording. Today we have something more effective, the financial restriction. On page 10 of the estimates for 1955-56 we have the following figures. In the year 1955-56 we are being asked for $1,807,825. The 1954-55 figure was $2,464,844, which represents a decrease of $657,019. The B.B.C. is spending some $18 million; the "Voice of America" is spending a far larger amount. We intend to spend only $1,807,825 in the next fiscal year.
There is one thing that I think every hon. member should understand, and also the experts in the Department of External Affairs; namely that the international service of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation could be a more effective agency than either the B.B.C. or the "Voice of America". Those forces who

are opposed to us have been able to build up effective resistance to the B.B.C. and "Voice of America". In the target areas the people have been led to believe that the "Voice of America" and the B.B.C. are the voices of great powers hungry for more power and with colonial design. But surely no one by the widest stretch of the imagination can make that charge against Canada, which has an honourable and excellent record. Therefore the messages we send over the international service have a very deep psychological meaning for people in the target areas, much more so than the messages which come over the B.B.C. or the "Voice of America".
Therefore it is essential that the international service be maintained and encouraged in order that we may have contact with and assist the morale of these people behind the iron curtain. Listen to the broadcasts from Bucharest, Warsaw and Kiev or any of these other places, and compare them with ours. On the one hand we hear militant, strong, persuasive broadcasts from communist countries. Our broadcasts are meek, mellow and lack courage, in many cases neglecting completely the psychological background of the people. These people are interested in receiving certain messages from us. It is not a message on the merits of democracy and why our way of life is better than theirs. They are not interested in having a cold analysis of the news or hearing about wild and animal life in Canada. They are vitally interested in hearing what our verdict is as to their present status of enslavement.
Our minister of external affairs is an affable diplomat of whom we are all very proud, and he knows that one of the purposes of diplomacy is to win friends. It may not always be possible to win the friendship of those whose ideology is different from ours, but we should try to maintain the friendship of those whose aims and interests are identical to our own, which are compelling reasons for friendship.
We are glad to hear the announcement by the Prime Minister on May 19 that it is intended to set up a commission to study some of the problems of radio and television in Canada, and we hope that commission will make recommendations which will remove many of the iniquities which exist at the present time and will provide for a greater utilization of Canadian talent.

Mr. Chairman, during world war II I had the privilege of serving with the Canadian night fighter squadron. The slogan of that squadron was "Midnight is our noon". I can only hope that the spirit behind those words will enlighten the chamber here tonight notwithstanding the lateness of the hour. The 50433-434
Supply-National Revenue full report of the deliberations of the committee on broadcasting is available to hon. members; therefore we do not need to indulge in needless repetition. My reason for rising at this time is some of the things that have been said thus far. I want to make it clear that I do not subscribe to the viewpoint expressed by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort, which he described as the position of the official opposition.
During any discussion on Canadian broadcasting it is always said that members of the official opposition are critical of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, but I have never expressed that viewpoint and so far as I know neither has any other spokesman for this party. We are fully aware of the outstanding work of the C.B.C. in pioneering broadcasting in this country. One point we have made is the necessity for changing our approach to broadcasting matters with changing circumstances and changing situations. Since broadcasting activities were formally launched in Canada there have been tremendous social changes, not only here but throughout the world.
Today we must recognize that broadcasting is a mature medium of publication, and we must recognize the principle of the freedom of publication. I agree with the viewpoint expressed by the hon. member for Edmonton West, that the quicker we get away from state domination of broadcasting the better it will be for the principles of liberty and freedom, especially freedom of publication. Dr. Marcus Long is a frequent commentator on the C.B.C. and does an excellent job. He put the problem in the proverbial nutshell when speaking to the board of trade in Toronto, when he warned of the danger of change in the concept of the state from servant to master. I am quoting him directly. He said:
Let us resist as we would the devil every effort of government to demand more control than it actually needs. Government must rest on the consent of the governed, working for the general good of all.
That sounds like a very good Liberal principle, in the old sense of the term.
Like other members of the committee, I enjoyed very much the experience. It is always an interesting experience to examine close up the very complex activity that C.B.C. broadcasting has developed into at the present time. I must admit that I found the committee work very exhausting and very time consuming, and I do not doubt that the officials of the C.B.C. were under the same impression. We spent a long time in an exhaustive analysis and examination of broadcasting activities.

Supply-National Revenue
That is very interesting, of course, but I fail to see why it should be necessary for members of parliament to become experts in the delicate art of ballet dancing and the provision of dramatic presentations and spectacles for the entertainment of the Canadian public. Unfortunately, with the present regulation system that is the role members of this house have to assume. I feel-and I think there are many others of the same opinion- that C.B.C. will be happier and certainly we would have more time at our disposal to deal with matters more directly associated with legislative activities, if we could get away from this partisan collision that is bound to occur if C.B.C. insists on continuing its multiple role of broadcaster, competitor, adjudicator, and so forth.
I am convinced that one way to get around this difficulty, as we have gotten around the difficulty in other crown corporations, is to establish some independent regulatory board that can stand apart in the broadcasting field and give an impartial adjudication and regulation of both our public broadcasting activities and the activities of the very influential and effective group of private broadcasters at the present time.
So far as the genial chairman of the committee is concerned, the hon. member for Portneuf, I must say he was absolutely amazing in the fairness he manifested as we wound our tortuous way through the examination of the annual report of the C.B.C., and he provided every opportunity for a complete discussion. Any fear of the deprivation of the rights of minority groups, I am convinced, could be easily taken care of by an impartial regulatory body. It is the solution that has been applied with other crown corporations. The problem of an approach to crown corporations is one of increasing complexity, and I think we could well support the principle of an independent regulatory body.
I said that circumstances have changed in this country. They have changed in other parts of the world also. I was interested in an article that told of recent developments in television activities in the United Kingdom. The problem there is much simpler than ours, because they have a homogenous population. They have a very small country, but with the advent of television and the problems created by that medium they have seen the necessity for breaking the complete monopoly of the B.B.C. and establishing an independent television authority that will be responsible for the commercialized private television activity recently launched in the United Kingdom.

If that change has been necessary in broadcasting in that comparatively small country, obviously we are forced to face up to changes in the situation here in Canada. In the committee deliberations it was obvious that the cost of programming television was becoming prohibitive when the responsibility rested entirely with the public broadcasting activity of C.B.C. Public opinion is gradually coming to realize this problem. Those who are closer to the situation realize that we have the lion by the tail, and if we are not careful it is going to run away with us.
I am convinced, as I read comments on broadcasting matters in Canada from time to time, even from within the Liberal party itself, that public opinion is eventually going to bring about the obvious changes that are necessary at this time. I feel there is a need for a comprehensive review of broadcasting in Canada, and I sincerely hope that the commission to be appointed will have complete freedom to undertake such a review and bring down the recommendations necessary for bringing our broadcasting policy up to date.
I do not wish to get into a long discussion at this late hour, but I should mention that some of the usual red herrings have been raised in this debate tonight; the fear of crass commercialism, the fear of infiltration and saturation by United States cultural influences, the failure to get down to the grass roots of cultural development in this country, and so forth, which according to this approach to the problem would be the result if we were to allow the private broadcasters an equal competitive opportunity with public broadcasting in this country.
So far as infiltration and saturation by United States influences are concerned, today Canada has reached sufficient maturity in its development toward nationhood to be completely recovered from the feeling of insecurity and inferiority in this regard that existed before world war II. As a matter of fact, we have now reached sufficient national and cultural maturity that we are beginning to make some cultural impact on our powerful neighbour to the south. That fact came out in the committee on broadcasting when the chairman of the C.B.C. board indicated that there is an increasing demand for some of Canada's outstanding programs.
So far as the use of T.V. programs of United States origin is concerned, even under the present circumstances we are dependent upon that source of supply to the extent of 50 per cent of our T.V. programs. I do not think the establishment of an independent, regulatory body would have any undesirable influence in that direction.

A comment was made that private broadcasters have made little contribution toward the development of talent in this country. If we examined the matter closely I think we would find that a good percentage of the talent engaged in C.B.C. radio activities, as well as in television activities today, began and had its early training in the small local broadcasting stations, all of which, of course, are operated on a private basis. Because of the lack of programming scope in the private stations they have little access to the network. For example, there is not much stimulus or encouragement for elaborate programming of the spectacle-drama type. The talent, beginning in the local communities, is obliged to move to the big cities which, under our present scheme of broadcasting, have become the production centres.
So much for the problems of talent and American infiltration. I should like to deal with the problem of crass commercialism which was the bugbear of broadcasting in its early infancy, particularly when the Canadian broadcasting commission was first established in 1932. As a result of the United States situation, broadcasting had become the drudge of the hucksters and quite definitely the commercial influence was undesirable indeed. But now that approach to the broadcasting media has changed as well, and we find that even the C.B.C. is not averse to having its programs sponsored. Indeed, I directed to the chairman of the board a question with regard to the excellent "Wednesday Night" series which aims at a program of outstanding excellence, and the chairman of the board was quite frank in indicating that, if possible, they would have no objections to having C.B.C. "Wednesday Night" sponsored. Of course with the comparatively new medium of television, commercialism has become developed to a high art and as with advertising in that other important medium of publication, namely the newspapers, I feel that the approach to television advertising has reached a fairly high level.
At this point I should like to indicate that in the past two years something remarkable has been developing in the Canadian film industry. We have now had television for two years, and I have been quite amazed to read that in that short interval a new, healthy, thriving film industry has been developed in Canada. For example, in 1952 there were only 23 Canadian film companies operating in that field. Today there are 46 film companies operating, mainly engaged in supplying the voracious appetite of Canada's television broadcasting system. The statistics pointing to the output of films are extremely interesting. Under the heading of commercial film 50433-434J
Supply-National Revenue production of special advertisements and so on, we find that in 1952 the Canadian industry produced 111 films; in 1953, 191, and in 1954, 600. There was a tremendous increase in two years. Actually they are taking over the United States control of this field. Back in 1952, because of its head start-it will be recalled that television was late in developing in Canada-the United States film industry had almost a complete monopoly. Today Canada is moving ahead quickly in this field. As to slide films, in 1952, 31 were produced; in 1953, 48; and in 1954, 100. Then a most important commercial film activity is this one described as "Others"; that means the more ambitious film productions. In 1952 there were none; in 1953, 50, and in 1954, 200. The trend is ever onward and upward. I feel that development of this kind is encouraging indeed, so far as Canadian cultural contributions to the film and T.V. media are concerned. It shows that Canada has reached a level of maturity and a level of confidence where it can successfully compete with more powerful television film industry activities to the south of us.
To bring these remarks to a conclusion, may I say this. From listening to government spokesmen and to spokesmen from the C.C.F. party I would conclude that they see no need for change in our broadcasting policy at the present time. I can understand that attitude coming from the C.C.F. group, because any group subscribing to a doctrinaire viewpoint sets out for itself an ideological target which encompasses all the activities in a nation. Having set out the target of rigid state control for our broadcasting medium and having achieved that target, there is the tendency to feel that no change is desirable.
I trust, Mr. Chairman, that in these brief remarks I have indicated that the situation today is a far cry from the situation that existed in 1932. In 1932 broadcasting was in its infancy. We subscribed to the theory of what was called natural monopoly, or that broadcasting was a natural monopoly because of its very nature. We thought private broadcasting would wither away and that public broadcasting would come into complete possession of the field. Recent statistics, of course, refute that claim, because in 1953 there were 140 private radio stations; in 1954, 144; and in 1955, 155 private broadcasting stations.
I should like to emphasize also that Canada has grown up since 1932. If we went back to 1932 and recalled our attitude toward international affairs in that pre-war period, I am sure we would realize that the situation today has changed completely in all respects. Canada's role in world war II established her

Supply-National Revenue as a nation among the nations of the world. We no longer need to be afraid of being submerged by any other cultural influence to the south of us. Neither do I think we should be afraid of so-called powerful financial interests in the private broadcasting field. I have greater confidence in the public of Canada than to feel that they are out deliberately to demoralize or debase the national life of this country. Yet that is the implication that rests continually upon the situation when we find our public broadcasting activities under the C.B.C. retaining an absolute and complete regulatory control over its competitors. I believe that as Canadians can be trusted to do a good job in other activities in Canada under impartial regulation by an independent board, they can also do a worthwhile and public-spirited job in the field of broadcasting.
On the other hand, if public morality cannot be trusted, which is the implication in maintaining rigid state control, I would also suggest that no amount of regulation and control by the state will solve the problem. I have a quotation that I think will illustrate this point. It is entitled "The Spirit of Liberty" and reads:
Liberty lies in the hearts of men and women; when it dies there, no constitution, no law, no court can save it; no constitution, no law, no court can even do much to help it. And what is this liberty which must lie in the hearts of men and women? It is not the ruthless, the unbridled will; it is not freedom to do as one likes. That is the denial of liberty, and leads straight to its overthrow.
The spirit of liberty is the spirit which is not too sure that it is right; the spirit which seeks to understand the minds of other men and women; the spirit which weighs their interests alongside its own without bias;-
I think notwithstanding the charges and accusations made against the private operators in this field, they are activated by the same high principle as are the private operators of newspaper publications today. I trust, Mr. Chairman, that even at this late hour the slogan I enunciated at the beginning of my remarks, "Midnight is our noon", will become a reality as we proceed to an examination of this important problem.

Listening to the remarks made earlier by the hon. member for Eglinton I felt that once again we were seeing an exhibition of the chief indoor sport of Tory politicians in Canada, sniping at the C.B.C. I was very pleased that the leader of our group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, placed on the record some of the facts regarding the background of our national radio system in Canada. It is rather amusing to tie in the arguments now advanced by the members of that group with

the remarks made by their former leader at the time the national radio system was set up in Canada.
On May 18, 1932, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett moved the second reading of Bill No. 4 in respect to radio broadcasting. At that time Mr. Bennett said, as reported at page 3035 of Hansard for May 18, 1932:
-X desire to intimate to the house that in a general way it follows the committee's report which was unanimously adopted a few days ago and it is based upon principles which the government believes should be adopted, because they fulfil two essential requirements without which radio broadcasting in Canada must fail in service to the Canadian people.
Then the prime minister went on to point out some of those essentials for a national radio system. He said:
First of all, this country must be assured of complete Canadian control of broadcasting from Canadian sources, free from foreign interference or influence. Without such control radio broadcasting can never become a great agency for the communication of matters of national concern and for the diffusion of national thought and ideals, and without such control it can never be the agency by which national consciousness may be fostered and sustained and national unity still further strengthened.
Then the prime minister went on to point out the second essential of a national radio system. He said:
Secondly, no other scheme than that of public ownership can ensure to the people of this country, without regard to class or place, equal enjoyment of the benefits and pleasures of radio broadcasting. Private ownership must necessarily discriminate between densely and sparsely populated areas. This is not a correctable fault in private ownership; it is an inescapable and inherent demerit of that system.
Then Mr. Bennett added the third essential. He said:
Then there is a third reason to which I might refer, and one which I believe must commend itself to every hon. member in this chamber. The use of the air, or the air itself, whatever you may please to call it, that lies over the soil or land of Canada is a natural resource over which we have complete jurisdiction under the recent decision of the privy council. I believe that there is no government in Canada that does not regret today that it has parted with some of these natural resources for considerations wholly inadequate and on terms that do not reflect the principle under which the crown holds the natural resources in trust for all the people. In view of these circumstances and of the further fact that broadcasting is a science that is only yet in its infancy and about which we know little . . .
He goes on to point out some further considerations. I think I have read enough into the record to indicate that when national radio was first introduced in this country by a Conservative government, the Conservative prime minister laid down certain essential conditions under which radio must be developed in this country. It is rather strange today to find Conservative

members attacking the very principle upon which the Canadian radio system was first established. We find that at that time there was widespread support for this principle of public ownership of radio.
Immediately after Mr. Bennett, Hon. Ernest Lapointe spoke very briefly. He said:
I just wish to endorse the views expressed by my right hon. friend the prime minister and to say that I am in full accord with the principle embodied in this bill. I have been supporting this principle from the first, more particularly after the work of the Aird commission, but I knew the difficulties in the way and the strength of the propaganda carried on to prevent the work of that commission from having the results which we witness today.
Then Mr. Lapointe was followed by Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, the late leader of this group. He said:
I should just like to associate myself with the last speaker (Mr. Lapointe) in congratulating the prime minister on his promptness in bringing down this bill to implement the report which has been unanimously adopted.
In view of the conditions laid down by the Conservative prime minister of that day it is difficult to understand the change in attitude on the part of members of that party. It appears that the burden of their argument against the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation centres around the question of a separate regulatory body. There were many representations made about radio broadcasting to the Massey commission, and its report dealt with the question of a separate regulatory body. You will find that on page 285 of that report the commission points out:
The chief demand of private broadcasters is that in place of the present system of control exercised by the board of governors of the C.B.C., a new and separate body should be set up to regulate all broadcasting in Canada. There is a difference of opinion on the powers which it should exercise. Some suggest that it should have powers equivalent to those of the present board of governors; others have in mind something like the federal communications commission of the United States. Others again think that such control might be too irksome, an opinion shared by some American broadcasters.
And then later:
We have considered these proposals and find that they would either divide and destroy, or merely duplicate the present system of national control. Legislation to set up a separate regulatory body would alter the present national system and would result in two independent groups of radio broadcasting stations, one public and one private. The C.B.C. would no longer have the control over all clear channels considered necessary to ensure national coverage.
I think, without going further into the recommendations of the commission, that in view of the widespread representations made to that commission by interested parties, and after having given the matter very careful
Supply-National Revenue consideration, the committee has made a report which sets forth my own personal views regarding this matter of a separate regulatory body.
I realize that the C.B.C. is under constant attack. I am also aware of the fact that it is not in a position to answer many of the attacks made upon it. In this country there has been a great deal of lobbying and a great deal of pressure exercised on parliamentarians. There has been much effort to propagandize the people of Canada on behalf of private broadcasters. Certainly we continually find in our newspapers editorials and news items attacking the C.B.C. In view of the fact that there is a close tie-up between the ownership of many newspapers in this country and the ownership of many privately-owned radio stations, one can perhaps understand the point of view of some of the daily newspapers. Going through our weekly newspapers in Canada I have found that, in the main, many have not seen fit to editorialize on matters of national concern. That is, they write their editorials about local conditions. Nevertheless they seem to have the habit of coming out every month or so with an editorial against the C.B.C.
It seems difficult to believe that this is spontaneous. Newspapers which would not bother to publish editorials dealing with the plight of agriculture in the district, and which would not see fit to editorialize in respect of matters brought before parliament, seem to have the habit of coming out with editorials directed against the C.B.C., and that organization is not in a position to answer those criticisms. They are obliged to take them without any effective means of answering. And indeed they could answer, I am sure they could, and quite adequately.
The fact that the C.B.C. is criticized is a reflection on the nature of that body. The national radio set-up in Canada seeks to cater to the needs of Canadians generally. We have varied tastes in what we want to hear on the radio and see on television. It would be utterly impossible for any radio body, either public or private, to satisfy all the people in Canada at any one time. I have heard the criticism that their programs are too cultural, that they are trying to force culture down our throats. Last year we heard the Leader of the Opposition make disparaging references to the wrestling matches on Saturday night. Well, I believe the C.B.C. carries wrestling matches on Saturday night because the great majority of the people want to watch wrestling on television and I happen to belong to that majority. I must say, however, that when they were bringing wrestling from Hollywood I thought many of the wrestlers

Supply-National Revenue would have been more qualified for Oscars to reward their acting than for any prowess they displayed as athletes. But it is a good show, and many people like to watch wrestling on television.
The C.B.C. is in an impossible position when it tries to meet the requirements and the wishes of all our people. But I wish to say this, that if we had no C.B.C., if everything were left to the control of the private broadcasters, this difficulty would not disappear. As a matter of fact I believe there would be a tendency to cater to the needs of one section of the population as opposed to another.
Many people like chamber music. On the other hand there may be a greater number who do not. It would be impossible for any radio body to satisfy the tastes of all the people in Canada, but I think the C.B.C. has done an excellent job. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris referred a moment ago to C.B.C. "Wednesday Night". That program is designed to provide the type of entertainment desired by a great many people, perhaps far more than are revealed in surveys. But I think that by and large the C.B.C. has done an excellent job in providing a varied bill of fare, if we may describe it in that way, for Canadian radio listeners and television viewers.
I do wish to make one reference to the work of the C.B.C., because as a teacher I am keenly aware of the importance of audiovisual aids to education, and I would be remiss if I did not commend the C.B.C. upon the excellence of its performances. One who has tried to teach English literature-Hamlet, Macbeth, Julius Caesar and other programs of that kind-appreciates the excellence of those programs. Indeed, it would be difficult to assemble more talented casts anywhere.
Many who are prone to criticize the C.B.C. would reveal a better spirit if they were to utter some praise for that organization. The thing that impresses me is that many of those who are so prone to criticize the C.B.C. are those who find no good in it; and I always suspect the person who can find only fault whether it be in relation to the C.B.C. or anything else. The fact that the C.B.C. is trying to serve the needs of the people of Canada leaves it in a position where it is open to criticism. It would be strange indeed if it were not criticized. They are condemned if they do and condemned if they don't. In all seriousness we have to ask ourselves this. If there were no C.B.C. and if radio were commercially controlled and operated, would we not have these difficulties?
I hear a good deal of talk about the standards of radio entertainment in the United States. Well, from the little television I have


seen in that country I have not been overly impressed. One need only consult the logs of television stations to the south of us to find that some of them have an early movie at seven o'clock and a late movie at 10.30, and they also have great amounts of advertising. And when one comes to size up the programming he realizes just how little there is in it unless, of course, he wishes to watch some old Hollywood movies that were put out many years ago, or class C productions made especially for television.
Some reference has been made in this debate to the talks heard over the C.B.C. In a democratic society we should be doing all within our power to encourage varied points of view. I would dread the thought of a society in which there was not a clash of opinion. The Leader-Post in my own constituency at one time carried at the top of its editorial page the slogan, "Where we all think alike no one thinks very much". It is quite amazing to hear some members of the committee suggest that the C.B.C. should not be allowed to carry certain talks because they do not find favour with a particular group. I for one am happy to hear points of view with which I disagree. Certainly in listening to the C.B.C. talks I find myself in diasgree-ment with many speakers. At the same time it is a challenge; it is stimulating to hear a point of view which does not coincide with your own. Perhaps we learn a great deal more from hearing the opinions of others, and it would be rather difficult to tie in our belief in democracy with a desire to exercise some sort of thought control.
The suggestion was made, why does the C.B.C. not check on what those people are going to say; why do they not keep them off the air? As much as I might disagree with a point of view, that person has the right to express his point of view. That is the strength of our democratic society. We maintain that our way of life is superior because we have free speech. In our society men may differ, and therein lies the strength of that society. If we are to succumb to the very virus which has destroyed democratic institutions in other parts of the world, then we are losing in the ideological war. In the struggle between rival ideologies our job is to convert them to our way of thinking, and not to adopt their methods. When we try to exercise some measure of thought control, then we are adopting the very methods which we abhor in others. I for one am only too happy that various points of view are expressed on our national radio.
With respect to our radio policy, it is important to remember that the conditions laid

down by the late R. B. Bennett still exist today. The very reasons he gave for the public ownership of our radio facilities in this country are as valid today as they were in 1932. These conditions have not changed. Apparently the opinions of the Conservatives have changed, but not the conditions under which the radio system was established.
When we hear a member of this house suggest that the government is following C.C.F. policy in carrying on the administration of the C.B.C., we need only go to the records of this house. I would suggest that some of my friends in the Conservative party go back and read through the debates at the time our national radio system was set up, and they will see only too clearly the valid reasons given by the late R. B. Bennett for the establishment of the Canadian radio commission on the basis of public ownership. I could read further remarks made by the late R. B. Bennett which indicate his views. For example, on page 3036 of Hansard he said:
Then there follows, of course, the provision for the commission expropriating stations when it is in a position financially so to do.
At that time there was no doubt whatever in the minds of the Conservatives and the government itself.

At that time there was universal agreement, as I pointed out a moment ago. After the late R. B. Bennett had put the government's position on the record, the late Ernest Lapointe rose in his place and congratulated the prime minister of the day. He was in complete agreement with everything the government was doing in the field of radio. We had agreement expressed by the leader of the C.C.F. party, the late J. S. Woodsworth. Members of the House of Commons were in complete accord as far as our national radio policy was concerned.
We heard the hon. gentleman the first time; he does not need to repeat it.

No one can suggest that I have been unduly prolonging the debate by speaking slowly and deliberately.

I pointed out earlier that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was under almost continuous attack by the private broadcasters, and quite naturally. After all,

Supply-National Revenue that is their business. They are out to expand and get into the lucrative field of radio advertising. I do not think there is any dearth of applications for private radio stations, and it is not a question of risk capital at all. It is understandable why the private broadcasters are out to sabotage the C.B.C., because they are looking after their own interests.
The C.B.C. is doing adequate work, but it is not in a position where it can defend itself. It should be remembered that this radio system was set up with the widespread support of all parties in the House of Commons. I think it is the duty of members of parliament to point out the good work being done by the C.B.C. Those who attack the C.B.C. should do so in a more constructive manner. The director of the private broadcasters said public opinion was such that something should be done, but it has been a deliberate policy on their part to sell the idea that there is something obnoxious about the C.B.C., that it is to be abhorred, that it is a monopoly.
We know there is a monopoly in the United States, though they have a number of networks all privately-owned. People say that the C.B.C. costs the taxpayer money, while the private companies could put out programs for nothing. All of us are taxpayers and consumers, and everybody who buys a bar of soap is helping to pay for the soap operas; and this would include those who do not own radio or television sets. It is a most absurd notion people have that a program is not being paid for in one way or another. It is, and it could not be otherwise.
With a publicly-owned system the people would have some measure of control, and such a system would be amenable to the wishes of the people. In my judgment this government has not played fair with the C.B.C. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar pointed out that at one time certain regulations were in effect, but they exist no longer. There is no doubt that the private stations want to set up their own networks. In that connection the Massey report has this to say at page 287:
We have also received from individual broadcasters, and from the British Columbia association of broadcasters, a request for the removal of restrictions on private networks, a request not formally made by the national body, the Canadian Association of Broadcasters. At present, private stations may receive special permission to form local networks only, and a very few are permitted to have affiliations with American networks: but the general principle is maintained that the private station be operated only for local services and as an outlet for national programs.

Then they go on to say:
The general effect of private network broadcasting would, we believe, be the same as that of a separate regulatory body. It would destroy the national system.
When people advocate a separate regulatory system they are advocating the destruction of the national system.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few brief remarks in reply to some of the things that have been said during the course of the debate. I am sure all members of the government and all government supporters will be grateful to the socialist member who has just concluded his speech for the strong endorsement he has given of government policy in connection with the C.B.C., radio broadcasting and television.
I wish to deal with the remarks made this evening by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who committed a most horrible distortion of what I had said and what the party for which I was speaking contends for in regard to a separate regulatory tribunal. During my 10 years in the house I have never heard a more misleading speech than that made tonight by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. He set up a series of straw men which bore no resemblance whatever to anything that had been said, and then proceeded to demolish them with great vigour.
Let me make it abundantly clear that in regard to the proposal for an independent regulatory body, we have stated in categorical terms that the two functions of the C.B.C. should be separated. Those two functions are, first, programming and operation of the national system of broadcasting; second, the regulation of all other forms of broadcasting in Canada.
Let me make it as clear as I can that we propose no change whatever in the first function. In other words the publicly-owned system would continue as a publicly-owned system. The C.B.C. would have the same operating system as at the present time. It would operate the present national system and its programs. The change would be in relation to the second function, which we propose should be transferred to another public body.
Therefore what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had to say, in conjuring up all kinds of results affecting the operation of the national system and its programs, has no relation to fact and no basis in reality. It has no proper place in the debate.
He mentioned the development of Canadian talent. In the system we propose the C.B.C. would have the same opportunity as heretofore to develop Canadian talent. The C.B.C.

has done good work in the development of Canadian talent. The private stations have also done good work in the development of Canadian talent.
I would remind the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that the C.B.C. itself in television was not able to put the proportion of Canadian television programs at more than 50 to 55 per cent of the total. The spokesman of the Canadian association of broadcasters contended that the private stations, if they were given licenses, would be prepared to do the same.
Second, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar talked about the opportunity we have under the C.B.C., and would not have under the proposal that the Conservatives have put forward, to hear grand opera and symphony music. What a distortion! Many of the symphonies that are listened to in this country are of United States origin. Whatever the C.B.C. is doing in this respect as part of its programming functions it will continue to do under the system we propose.
Then we hear that we must keep the system Canadian. We of the Conservative party have nothing to learn from any other party in that respect, least of all from these socialists. These assertions by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar completely fall to the ground, because no change has been proposed in this respect.
As to the second function of the C.B.C., in relation to the licensing, regulation and control over all other forms of broadcasting, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says, "Let us keep the licensing under public control". That is precisely what we propose. The tribunal we propose is a public body. That idea has not sunk into the minds of these socialists. If they would stop talking long enough to learn from other people, they might grasp the facts, but they will not listen to explanations of the facts.
Second, he asks that we preserve public control. That is precisely what we propose.
The third thing he said was that we must keep parliament in control. There is no more effective way of keeping parliament in control than through the establishment of the kind of public regulatory body we recommend. It is the most direct form of assertion of control through proper parliamentary means. The hon. member who puts forward this suggestion supports the kind of policies that have sought to take further and further away from parliamentary control the financing and operations of the C.B.C. The Progressive Conservative party has insisted in season and out of season on the maintenance of strict parliamentary control, and we have had no
