As one might expect, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar took advantage of the opportunity given to him tonight to distort the position of the Progressive Conservative party in this matter, and to make as well an attack on the private stations. If the private stations of this country, which have rendered an important service, as every one of us in his local community knows, looked to the C.C.F. for any measure of justice, they would go without any justice whatever. They have had nothing but antagonism and bitter attacks from the socialists at all times.
We in the Progressive Conservative party do not like private chains and we do not like the idea of stations falling into the same powerful hands. The kind of proposal we have put forward would help to arrest that kind of threat that has gone on under the present system, which is supported by the socialists. When they talk about these powerful financial interests; when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar lets the chills run up and down his own spine by this blood-curdling expression, he fails to see that that sort of thing is going on under the system he supports.
Of course, democracy has no place in the thoughts and the approach of the socialists. There has been little enough of it in the approach of the government. You would think the fact that people have certain preferences in regard to the programs they wish to hear has no place in the thoughts of these socialists. They are so bent on regimentation of the thinking and even the listening of the Canadian public that they have very little patience to expend on people who prefer to hear other kinds of programs.
I would say to these socialists that they can take any kind of recognized listener interest survey they choose, and they will find that in the areas where there are private stations that are permitted to have power comparable with that of the C.B.C. stations, the private stations outrank the C.B.C. stations in listener popularity. Not only does that

Supply-National Revenue apply to television but to radio broadcasting as well. It would pay them to read some of the evidence given to the committee. They would find that in the city of Toronto, for instance, United States television stations take about two-thirds of the listener interest. That is the kind of system they wish to perpetuate.
In conclusion I should like to say this. I have listened to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar make many speeches on radio in the committee in earlier years and more recently in the house itself. I have never heard him make a speech on radio when he did not refer to the part Mr. Bennett played in the establishment of the national system of broadcasting, for it was he who set it up in 1932. In the eyes of the C.C.F. in this one particular Mr. R. B. Bennett is a saint, but in every other reference of the socialists to Mr. Bennett you would think there is nothing of sainthood about him, for they have nothing but words of denunciation for the same man.
I wish they would get the facts straight. What Mr. Bennett did was to set up a national system of broadcasting in Canada because, under the circumstances obtaining in 1932, it was the only means for providing not just the metropolitan areas but all of Canada with a national Canadian system. That is the system he sought to set up, and it is the kind of system that I think is supported by all the members of this house today. I do not know of anybody in this house who proposes that the national broadcasting system should be displaced. Certainly we do not propose that. We are proposing changes in the function of the C.B.C. in relation to other forms of broadcasting. I hope I have made that point clear to all concerned.
Mr. Chairman, we hear complaints and bleatings from the socialists about attacks on the C.B.C. May I say that there have not been attacks on the C.B.C. in this house tonight, and that there have been few attacks on the C.B.C. at any time in previous debates. What this house has heard have been attacks on the weaknesses of the system, and attacks on government policy supported by the C.C.F. That is what has been heard.
I shall conclude by saying this. When the socialists say that the C.B.C. has no opportunity to answer attacks they are just doing plain violence to the facts, because the C.B.C. has always had full opportunity before this committee to make their statements with regard to this matter of policy.
What about before the general public?
Are you trying to regiment what the general public shall hear?
Oh, oh.

It is all part of this socialist thinking. Regimentation is part and parcel of their thinking, and we have these further evidences of it tonight. Indeed, they are superfluous.
The C.B.C. is afforded full opportunity in the committee to say what it wishes to say. There might be some in this house who might say that the kind of system of regulation is a matter of policy, and that it is not a proper matter for comment on the part of C.B.C. officials. We take that position with regard to government officials who appear before any committee. They are never permitted to be questioned with regard to policy or to state their opinions in that regard. But, Mr. Chairman, so far as I am aware-and I have been a member of the radio committee since 1945-no one has ever taken that position with regard to the C.B.C. Indeed, in every one of these committees Mr. Dunton has been asked for his comments on the proposal for setting up an independent regulatory tribunal, and has made his comments with full opportunity to say what he wished about it. Nobody has ever said him nay.
Therefore when the socialists try to give the impression that there is some kind of vendetta being carried on against the C.B.C., that there is some kind of injustice being perpetrated upon the C.B.C., or that there is some kind of scheme here for enthroning private interests and displacing the publicly-owned national system, they do violence to the facts.

I do not wish to speak at length at this time except to say that this debate, which has been extremely vigorous and forceful, has also been rather illuminating. I cannot help thinking that my friend the hon. member for Eglinton has not made much ground either in the house or in the press of the country. I just want to quote from an article that appeared in the Ottawa Journal of Saturday, April 2, 1955, entitled " 'Rights' to the Air". It reads as follows:
The Prime Minister has told parliament (taking a position against that of the Liberal Federation) he considers it neither desirable nor necessary that an independent board be set up to take over the general control of broadcasting now exercised by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to regulate not only private radio and television stations but the C.B.C. itself. That is the position to which The Journal invariably has given its support. Year after year this well-organized campaign of private interests against the supervisory authority of C.B.C. has been pursued with vigour and determination. Mr. St. Laurent, like his predecessors in office, is stoutly opposed to any clipping of the wings of C.B.C., but the strength behind the move for an independent board is illustrated by its ability to secure a majority in the Liberal federation itself against the wishes of the Prime Minister.

The basic issue is simple. Private interests do not possess and cannot possess any "rights" to the air. A private broadcasting interest cannot acquire anything more binding than a permit to use the airways-a permit subject to cancellation at any time by the constituted authority of the state itself. In other words a private broadcaster has a privilege but no vested interest.
That is a statement which should sink deeply into the minds of the members of this house.
This long campaign is aimed at putting C.B.C. and private interests on an equal footing and subject to the same regulation by an independent tribunal. In other words the private broadcasters thus would become endowed with vested rights to the air, which is what they have been striving for these many years. They then would occupy a position from which they could not readily be ousted-a place not subject to such effective disciplinary action as is afforded by present regulation under licence from C.B.C.
The private broadcasting interests have a good deal of influence, as this week's events have made clear. But Mr. St. Laurent's strong stand seems to leave the question settled for the moment. It would be an unfortunate day for the public if the campaign ever should succeed and obtain "rights" to the air.
I just quote that editorial to show that the press of this country are not behind what the hon. gentleman contends. Another editorial, one of April 1, 1955, shows that private broadcasters are under a false assumption entirely. This editorial reads as follows:
In the House of Commons, Prime Minister St. Laurent has given his personal opinion that a new tribunal to regulate broadcasting is neither desirable nor necessary. Many other Liberals will share his view, even though the advisory council of the national Liberal federation has recommended that the idea of some such tribunal be studied by a special commission. This idea of a "referee" is being propagated by private broadcasters who maintain, improperly, that they are in competition with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. If any real need were apparent, a commission might clarify matters. But so far parliament has felt competent to set the course of broadcasting policy.
After all, it is only a few years since the Massey commission was instructed as one of its tasks to consider "the principles upon which the policies of radio and television broadcasting should be based". On the basis of many briefs, public hearings, and its own investigations, it concluded that " the system recommended by the Aird commission (1929) has developed into the greatest single agency for national unity, understanding and enlightenment"
Private stations, the Massey report noted, were originally slated for elimination. But they have made a useful place for themselves within the national service. They have grown in numbers and wealth. At the same time, "the statement that the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is at once their judge and their business rival implies a view of the national system which has no foundation in law, and which has never been accepted by parliamentary committees or by the general public".
The Massey commission labelled as "false" the assumption that broadcasting in Canada is an
Supply-National Revenue industry. It declared that broadcasting is a national service and would be duplicated or destroyed if some new agency were set up. As the report concluded, the dangers of too much commercialism and too much American influence are even greater in television than in radio broadcasting. For still fewer channels are available, investment is heavier, and costs are higher, while many U.S. programs are cheap.
In the circumstances, the question is whether private or public interests are to be dominant in this field. Considerations of national policy indicate that private broadcasting should be subordinate to a national service, as is now the case.
I must say that personally I subscribe 100 per cent to those views. Radio broadcasting under the C.B.C. has been successful ever since its inauguration. It is a growing concern attempting to give the people of this country a national service from the Canadian point of view. I do not believe that position can be taken by private interests. I do not see that there is any necessity or likelihood of a private regulatory body being set up.
May I ask the minister who suggested a private regulatory body?

I meant to say an independent regulatory body. One of the recommendations of the Massey commission was that the whole subject of television and radio broadcasting in Canada be reconsidered by an independent investigating body not later than three years after the commencement of regular Canadian television broadcasting. The hon. member for Eglinton asked about this, and I am prepared to announce, on behalf of the government, that there will be either a commission or a board of inquiry set up some time within the near future to study the whole situation.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this has been a long debate. I am sure everyone is tired, and I think if you would call the estimates we might get along.

If the government is not prepared to make the required improvement or revision of its own policy, then at least, it is something that the government is prepared to appoint a royal commission to study the question and make recommendations. I should like to point out, and I do this with full respect for whatever may be the personnel of the royal commission-
I did not say a royal commission; I said a commission or board of inquiry.

My remarks will apply just the same. The value of an inquiry by a commission or a board of inquiry will depend very largely on the personnel. I hope the government will not overlook the opportunity of getting people with practical experience to sit on that commission or board of inquiry.

Would the minister say why the C.B.C. application for a television station in St. John's was turned down in favour of a private organization?

Just turn the dial and listen to it.

Regardless of what the member for Eglinton said about the situation in Toronto, I am confident the people of the lower mainland of British Columbia are pleased with the establishment of a C.B.C. television station. The United States stations have had a poor audience in Canada ever since.
That is not the evidence that was given to the committee.
I do not place too much confidence in evidence that is gathered by organizations that have a vested interest.
Not even if their services are subscribed for by the C.B.C. with the taxpayers' money?

I may not be so opposed to the hon. member for Eglinton if he will only hold his horses. Since there are around three-quarters of a million people in this area and television has become the accepted thing in the average home, can the minister say when another privately-owned television station might be authorized for the area?
You will have to change the policy and get away from a policy of monopoly.

Can the minister indicate whether it is the intention to set up a C.B.C. television station on Vancouver island?
There is not any intention at the moment of having a C.B.C. station on Vancouver island. But I have no doubt if there were an application for a private station it would be entertained.
But there are private stations on Vancouver island, are there not?
I thought the hon. member was referring to a television station.
I am.
There is no television station on Vancouver island.
Then we have to depend on United States stations.

I understand an application was made to the C.B.C. recently by private interests in Red Deer, Alberta, for a television station. Why was that application turned down? These people are being denied the right to view television and to have the enjoyment of television programs.

Would the minister consider having the C.B.C. set up some type of booster station in the area so these people may view their television programs from Edmonton or Calgary?
That would have to come before the board. I am not in a position to answer at the moment.

speechtext: It does not make them right; they are still wrong.

Let me continue. Nevertheless the figure of committals is hard to verify, because there are so many different ways of approaching them. While I am not undertaking to admit that these are wrong,
I am not for a moment trying to suggest that they are right. The thing that interests me, at any rate, is the probation figures, and there has been no suggestion that the probation figures are not right.
The matter with which I am concerned, as I say, is this question of probation. We have only about one-tenth the number of people being probated in Canada that they have in England and Wales, as against the fact that our population is about one-third of theirs. So I suggest we ought to have about one-third, if this thing had been going as I have suggested it should have been going. In England they have had astonishing success. Between 1907, when the probation of offenders act was passed, and 1937, when the late Lord Samuel in a speech took stock of the situation, the number of annual commitments to prison in England over this period of 30 years had been reduced from more than 180,000 to less than 60,000; and between 1937 and 1950 the figure had dropped to approximately 35,000. This is attributed largely to the effect of probation.
The next point I wish the committee to consider is the relative success of probation as against committal to prison. In England the figure given is that from 75 to 80 per cent of first offenders placed on probation are rehabilitated and do not offend again. On the other hand, the figure for repeaters in Canada as shown in the article by Professor Jaffary, in the penal reform magazine of Canada of the Canadian Bar Review, for November, 1949, is really staggering.
In Ontario male offenders are sent chiefly to two large institutions, namely the Ontario reformatory at Guelph for first offenders and those under 21 years, and the industrial farm at Burwash for repeaters. For the year 1947 the Guelph figures show that of 1,480 inmates some 750, or 51 per cent, were repeaters. At Burwash 1,005 of the 1,039 inmates were repeaters, or 97 per cent. But that, of course, is explained by the fact that it is a place for repeaters.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

I resent that very much. I have read the figure. The minister is now wanting to put an interpretation of his own on it. He can do that afterwards if he likes. I am reading these figures. A word is said about cost. The commission found there were some 8,000 recidivists or repeaters in Canada in 1936. Then the Ar-chambault commission carefully studied the costs of handling 188 of them, each of whom had had 10 or more convictions. The findings are startling. The convictions averaged 19 per individual. The cost of conviction was $18,000 per individual. I suppose that is

because they each had so many convictions. Maintenance costs in institutions, an average term of 11 years, added $7,450 per individual; the total cost was $25,450 per individual. Then he goes on and Professor Jaffary asks:
After spending this $25,000 per man on conviction and incarceration, what did we have to show for it? A confirmed criminal, hardened and antisocial, vowing further warfare on the community. Clearly, for all our profligate expenditure we are securing not protection but the reverse, further aggression. What kind of social policy is this?
I have dealt with the money side of these convictions, and I want to say just a word about the far-reaching moral side, the effect on the family of a convicted man, if he has a family; the stigma on the children, the support of the family while he is in jail, and the loss of his own pride.
I want to go back again to the question of probation. As I said, I think this question is a challenge to the conscience and common sense of all of us. That is the reason I am talking at this time of the night. I give as a comparison the population of England and Wales. We have little more than one-tenth of the number on probation. That is, we have 3,631 as against 33,929. I submit it would be reasonable to say that if we had dealt with the matter seriously in the sense of the Archambault report made 17 years ago, we would have approximately one-third of the number on probation. That is to say, since we have one-third of the population of England and Wales we would have one-third of the number of repeaters, or say 11,000. Therefore on this line of reasoning we have been sending to prison instead of probating some 7,000 people a year.
I am trying to make clear the basis on which I am putting this. I do not want to exaggerate it. The minister may say, "We would not have got up to that number so quickly." If he says that I would not be inclined to dispute it with him. This means on the reasoning I have been giving that some tens of thousands of people have gone to prison instead of being probated, since the Archambault report was made. As I shall point out, when the Archambault commission was appointed by the Department of Justice one of the things they were asked to do was report on probation, which they did do.
Then, having in mind the high ratio of success, 75 to 80 per cent in the case of probationers, and the poor record of those committed to prison, it is obvious that lamentable results follow. No wonder that Professor Jaffary in the Canadian Bar Review said:
Our Canadian system of handling offenders is fundamentally irresponsible, both in terms of money and in terms of human value.

I now wish to examine the record of the Department of Justice. In 1936-and I want to make very clear that this was a legacy left on the doorstep of the present minister;
I am not suggesting he is responsible for all this-the Archambault commission was appointed to report on, among other things: The conditional release of prisoners including parole or release on probation, conditional release under the Ticket of Leave Act and remission generally.
In 1938 the commission reported, and among other things recommended:
70. A probation system modelled on the system now in force in England should be adopted throughout Canada, both for adults and young offenders.
74. The pay and duties of probation officers should be the subject of an agreement between the provincial and federal authorities.
Writing in the Canadian Bar Review in November, 1949, Professor Jaffary, associate professor of the school of social work, University of Toronto, had this to say:
In Canada we have made little use of adult probation as a method of treatment.
At page 1040 Professor Jaffary says:
Why have we not used probation more?
Then he goes on to say:
Our Canadian system of handling offenders is fundamentally irresponsible. It is irresponsible because it is broken into so many separate bits and pieces that real responsibility cannot be placed. No one authority can be charged with the inefficiency of the system, with its high rates of recidivism, its wasteful costs. Hence, we have drifted-and are still drifting.
I now wish to go on and speak about the record of the federal government particularly. The Department of Justice, as was said on a famous occasion many years ago, has done too little and too late. The Archambault report was made in 1938, recommending strongly as I have indicated. So far as I can discover the federal government has done almost nothing over the past 17 years on this matter of probation.
I come to the committee to which the minister referred the other night. I am not overlooking that. So far as I can discover, the federal government has done almost nothing. When the minister was describing it the other night he took great unction to his soul because he appointed this commitee. The Archambault commission recommended in the strongest terms a widespread system of probation, and recommended officers jointly paid by the federal and provincial governments; yet so far as I can discover nothing has been done.
I cannot find that the provinces have been offered any encouragement, any guidance,

any financial assistance. According to the minister, what has been done is to set up an advisory committee. When the minister referred to it the other night as he did I was surprised to learn, as I did afterwards, that the committee apparently had not been asked to deal with probation at all. It goes far beyond the minister's period of office, but it does not go back beyond the government's period of office, about which we are so often reminded.
These extracts indicate that the minister seems to think that after 17 years, if they take preliminary steps to get the provinces together that is sufficient. I submit that the

report of the Archambault commission was a good one, and it was commissioned by the Minister of Justice. speechtext:
I shall be very glad to do that on some more suitable occasion. My hon. friend, however, is quite right in saying that the real issue in this matter is the question of how soon we can have the provinces of Canada instal systems of probation. My hon. friend has left the impression that the Department of Justice-not, as he has so charitably said, while I was minister-did nothing about the Archambault report. Well, let us look at the facts of the matter. The hon. member conceded that obviously very little could be done during the war in the implementation of the Archambault report; but he charges that since the end of the war the Department of Justice has done nothing.
I am speaking from memory, but I think the figures are correct. In April, 1946, Major General Gibson was appointed commissioner of penitentiaries and instructed to bring in a report as to the basis on which the recommendations of the Archambault commission could be implemented. He made his report in February, 1947, and the necessary legislation was introduced, passed and assented to in June, 1947, to become effective September 1, 1947.
Out of the 88 recommendations in the Archambault report, 68 involved action by the federal government. The other 20 involved either joint action with the provinces or were the sole responsibility of the provinces or of local communities. Of the 68 recommendations which called for action by the federal government, at least 54 have already been implemented or are now in the process of being carried out. It is the implementation of those recommendations which came under federal jurisdiction which has greatly improved the penal system of this country, as I am glad to see that my hon. friend from Greenwood concedes.
Apparently, however, my hon. friend's research did not disclose the fact that there was a dominion-provincial conference in 1947, one year after Major General Gibson had filed his report. There was a discussion at this conference as to the means by which the Archambault report could be implemented, both as regards those matters which came under the responsibility of the federal government and those matters which were

the responsibilities of the provincial governments. Very little progress was made at this conference. The purpose of the appointment of the Fauteux commission was to get a mass of data relating to probation.
That was six years later.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is quite true; but in the meanwhile the hon. member for Greenwood has left the impression that the provinces have no capacity for starting any probation system of their own, and that they are quite incapable of carrying out any recommendations of the Archambault commission for which they are constitutionally responsible. But the facts of the matter are that four or five of the provinces at the present time have made a respectable beginning on a probation system. One of the provinces my hon. friend from Greenwood has overlooked is his own province of Ontario.

I was talking about the
dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman from
Greenwood implies that we could not have a system of probation in the Canadian provinces except by the federal government prodding the provincial governments into discharging what is their responsibility and nobody else's. British Columbia, Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia have already begun without any inspiration on the part of the federal government provincial systems of probation. The Fauteux advisory committee was appointed to secure in an objective manner data which we hope will appeal to all the provinces of Canada and induce them to introduce provincial probation systems. As the hon. member for Greenwood has said, the results which have been obtained from probation in Great Britain and in other European countries have been spectacularly good.
It is perfectly clear that money invested in a probation system is much more efficiently invested than it would be in an increase in penitentiary or gaol accommodation. I said the other day that this is not a new subject. We have been conscious of its importance for some time; and it was with a view to persuading all the provinces to follow the example set by some of them that we are getting these data together. We hope to be able to persuade all the provinces to act.
There is no difference of opinion whatsoever between the hon. member for Greenwood and myself, as to the value of probation. My only purpose in rising is so that the record will not be left in the condition in which my hon. friend for Greenwood left it. He
Supply-Justice
has cast an aspersion on those preceding me in the Department of Justice on the ground alleged by him that inadequate steps had been taken to interest the provinces in probation. The facts are that as soon as the war was over, Major General Gibson was appointed as the very efficient commissioner of penitentiaries, and the necessary legislation was expeditiously introduced into parliament to implement the recommendations of the Archambault report for which the federal government was responsible.
One of the very first steps taken was a conference with the provinces in the fall of 1947 for the purpose of discussing the implementation of the Archambault report. That has been followed by the carrying out of probation in certain of the provinces, and the purpose of our present activities is to see that what was begun in four or five provinces should be extended to all of them. I cannot see that the Department of Justice at any stage has been remiss in the discharge of its duties.

This item states "discharge and transfer of inmates; compensation to discharged inmates". Would the minister say whether the penitentiaries are overcrowded, from what penitentiaries transfers have to be made to others, and what the government contemplates in the way of new buildings and arrangements for looking after prisoners and feeding them in a more modern manner, as recommended by the Archambault commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to transfers, my hon. friend will appreciate the fact that it is the total accommodation in all the penitentiaries of Canada which determines our ability to handle all the prisoners who come into any penitentiary for admission. Most of the transfers to which reference is made are transfers from either Quebec or Ontario, at the present time, to the western provinces in certain cases and to the maritime provinces in others. The larger centres of population in Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia are the ones which produce what might be described as surplus penitentiary population which has to be accommodated in other places where the local production of convicts is lower and where as a result they cannot fill their penitentiaries with local convicts. I am proud of the fact

Supply-Justice
that the part of Canada from which I come seems to be incapable of keeping our western penitentiaries full.
So far as new accommodation is concerned, our thought was to construct a penitentiary for women at Collins Bay with a view to the transfer of the women prisoners from the present building in which they are incarcerated at Kingston. This is a separate building, but one of the Kingston group. Then our plan is to use the vacated building at Kingston as a centre where we can take the prisoners when they come into the penitentiary in the first place, so they can be held there until we can determine in what part of the penitentiary itself they should go. This will help to avoid having younger offenders come into contact with older criminals.
In addition to that one new structure, we plan on having a larger penitentiary in eastern Canada, that is in either Quebec or Ontario, to take care of the growth in penitentiary population in that part of Canada, and another one in either Alberta or British Columbia, to take care of the growth in prison population there.
Might I ask the minister one more question. It says "compensation to discharged inmates". Is there any set rule as to how much a prisoner gets on discharge? How much money is used for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a set formula. In addition to that, the prisoner is paid for his work while he is in the penitentiary. He has any accumulated savings which are available from that source as well when he is discharged.

Are different types of work carried on in each penitentiary? For instance, I am thinking at the moment of Dorchester. What particular work is carried on there? Are any goods manufactured, or is farming carried on, or what is done?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, lacking at this late hour the assistance of my staff I am afraid I am not able personally to give any details with regard to the work at Dorchester or the other prisons; but such work varies from prison to prison. In some places, for example, there is a great deal of printed forms and other printed material prepared for use in the penitentiaries and ir other government departments. In other prisons, or perhaps in the same prison, we produce large quantities of prison clothing and shoes. In other prisons-and I think this is true of Dorchester to which the hon. gentleman has just referred-farming operations are carried out on a considerable scale. The total production for all the penitentiaries across

Canada runs into substantial sums of money under all these heads, and is quite an important source of revenue on the other side of the ledger to the moneys which we are obliged to expend to maintain the prisons.
I have just one more question. I take it that this production from the labour of the penitentiaries is sold more or less to the government and that it is not sold to the public. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, that is right. It is sold to other government departments. A great deal of it is used within the prison itself. For example, the consumption of food in our penitentiary system is very substantial. A very large percentage of it indeed is grown and prepared upon the penitentiary properties. The same thing is true with respect to clothing. A large percentage of it is manufactured in the penitentiaries.
Are the inmates credited with the amount of labour they do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are credited with wages for that labour.

Mr. Chairman, the reply the minister gave to the hon. member for Vic-toria-Carleton seems to be denied by a recent report from the province of Saskatchewan to the effect that the penitentiary at Prince Albert is somewhat overcrowded, and that fact has been part of the cause of the recent trouble there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. I cannot remember the figures exactly, but I think they were 660 and 630, if I am not mistaken. In other words, the capacity of the penitentiary at Prince Albert was 660 and its population was 630. It therefore could not have been overcrowded because that number would not even fill it to capacity, much less overcrowd it.
The trouble then was not due to overcrowding?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
What was given as the cause of the uprising? I understand that some conditions were not in line with ordinary procedure, and that they might have been short of staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, they were not overcrowded. They were not short of staff. They had had beforehand very few complaints of the character of those which are sometimes given by rioting convicts as the reason for their action. More than that, only a small percentage of the prisoners took part in the riot. I am sorry I cannot give now any more facts than these. We are having an investigation conducted at the present time by the
